**In this app:** `partial` — A real substitution, and nothing like the spray can in black the previous version of this record described. The gesture is two steps in one area: a click with no sample yet is an eyedropper that reads the active layer’s own pixels and stores the colour to replace (`ColorReplacementToolArea.tsx:108-116`), and every press after that opens a drag. The replacement colour is read off the live store at pointer-up (`ColorReplacementToolArea.tsx:141`) rather than mirrored into the args by a bar, so changing the foreground while the tool stays selected takes effect on the next stroke — which is why the options bar renders the foreground as a readout and writes no colour at all. What the commit writes is the substitution the tool is named for: `replaceColorPreservingLuminance` (`colorReplacement.ts:182`) applies a single luminance OFFSET, `out = replacement + (L − L_replacement)`, so each replaced pixel keeps its own shading and only its hue and chroma move. It edits the ACTIVE layer in place through `updateLayerByTool` (`ColorReplacementToolArea.tsx:166`) and never creates one, and Opacity is the strength of the substitution rather than a canvas `globalAlpha`, so a 50 percent replacement is a half-tint of the same shading rather than a half-transparent wash of a solid. Four of the controls are genuinely live and the region arithmetic behind them is real: Tolerance is a squared three-channel RGB distance, and Limits decides reach rather than membership, with Contiguous flooding out from every matching pixel the stroke touched, one call per region (`colorReplacement.ts:376-398`), and Discontiguous replacing only what is under the brush. Five things diverge. `Limits` offers two of Adobe’s three entries, so Find Edges is unreachable, and the second is spelled `Discontinuous` where Adobe writes `Discontiguous` (`ColorReplacement.tsx:22`). `Tolerance` is 0-100 on this tool’s own scale, converted before it reaches the shared fill code, against Adobe’s documented 0-255. `Sampling` is a real `disabled` select whose options are `Current Layer` and `All Layers` — neither of Adobe’s Continuous / Once / Background Swatch, and the app has no background color for Background Swatch to name — so the one control that decides which colour is the target cannot reach the tool at all. `Mode` and the Brush Preset Picker are absent, so the Color blend mode Adobe calls the reason this tool is a replacement is unreachable and there is no tip, and the top-bar Size slider the app renders in that position has no Photoshop counterpart on this bar at all — Adobe’s own manual opens the tool with “Choose a brush tip in the options bar” and never lists a Size — so it is capped at 200 px (`ColorReplacement.tsx:148`) rather than the 5000 the picker offers, and it is the app’s addition recorded here rather than in `options[]`. The bar also carries one control Photoshop does not have: `Smoothness` (`ColorReplacement.tsx:130-144`), a 0-50 feathering of the boundary the user can see, which is recorded here rather than in `options[]` because `types.ts` reserves that array for Photoshop’s own controls. Photoshop repaints the replaced pixels live as the stroke moves; the app draws no preview at all, for the reason its own tool area states — an honest overlay needs the full-layer plan recomputed on every pointer move. Its tool-select key is the one above, and the app agrees with it: the tool sits in the Brush group, so `B` reaches the slot and `Shift+B` cycles to it — the same binding the app already had. `AppKeyboardShortcuts.tsx` also lists it in the `tipSizeField` table, so `[` and `]` resize its tip and the `0` and `1` opacity rows apply here as they do on the Brush.

### Eraser Tool

`eraser` · **E**

Removes pixels to transparency along a stroke, in Brush, Pencil or Block mode, with per-stroke Opacity, per-dab Flow and Erase to History.

The Eraser removes pixels under a dragged tip, writing transparency on a layer and the background color on a Background layer or one whose transparency is locked. Its Mode chooses the tip: Brush is a soft round tip with adjustable hardness, Pencil is hard-edged, and Block is a fixed-size square with no opacity control at all. Opacity is a per-stroke ceiling as on the Brush, while Flow is the per-dab rate that builds erasure up within that ceiling. Erase to History turns the same drag into a restore, painting the area back to whichever state or snapshot is set in the History panel.

**Modifiers**

- **Alt** — While dragging, temporarily switches the stroke to Erase to History, restoring the area to the state or snapshot set in the History panel.
- **Shift** — Click once, then Shift-click a second point and the erase is drawn between the two as a straight line.

**Shortcuts**

- `E` — Selects the Eraser Tool.
- `Shift+E` — Cycles the slot shared with the Magic Eraser and the Background Eraser.
- `[` — Decreases the brush size to the next smaller preset diameter. On the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, Color Replacement Tool, Smudge, Dodge, Burn and Clone Stamp.
- `]` — Increases the brush size to the next larger preset diameter. On the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, Color Replacement Tool, Smudge, Dodge, Burn and Clone Stamp.
- `0` — Sets the brush Opacity to 100 percent. On the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, Color Replacement Tool and Clone Stamp.
- `1` — Sets the brush Opacity to 10 percent. On the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, Color Replacement Tool and Clone Stamp.

**In this app:** `partial` — The Eraser edits the active layer in place by subtracting alpha, which is the right model, and it produces exactly one history state per stroke because the commit is the pointer-up. A previous version of this record said the Mode list was Photoshop-shaped but not Photoshop-capable, because the `brush` option was rendered with Adobe’s real label and `disabled` on the DOM node and Hardness was absent for the same reason. Both halves of that are no longer true: `Eraser.tsx` offers Brush, Pencil and Block with none of them disabled, Brush mode reaches the shared stamped-dab tip engine through `eraseWithTip` (`eraser.ts:215`), and Hardness renders as a live slider in Brush mode wired through `handleHardnessChange`. Mode is therefore `present` and Hardness `partial` rather than `missing` — partial because the bar withholds it in Pencil mode, where Adobe’s page still lists Hardness among the four controls adjustable there and where the app’s Pencil mode is hard-edged by construction. Two app-only controls are on the bar and are recorded here rather than in `options[]`: a `Spacing` slider in Brush mode, wired to the tip engine’s spacing, which Adobe puts in the Brush Settings panel rather than on this bar, and the mode-gated rendering of Hardness itself. Size is capped at 500 px. Opacity is present and works as Photoshop’s per-stroke ceiling, and the control is correctly withheld in Block mode. Flow remains the notable finding: the bar renders Photoshop’s real `Flow` label over a 1–100 range and a hardcoded 100 percent value, and Adobe documents neither bound, but the input carries `disabled` and writes nothing, because Flow is a per-dab alpha ramp and one stamped pass cannot honour one. Airbrush, Smoothing and the two pressure toggles, Brush Angle, Erase to History and Symmetry are absent, and so is the Alt-drag temporary Erase to History gesture. The Shift straight-line constraint, by contrast, is implemented and is the one modifier row on this bar the app honours: `EraserToolArea.tsx` anchors the stroke on a plain click and draws from that anchor on a Shift-click, the two-click gesture Adobe describes. Because Brush and Pencil modes stamp through the tip engine, the tip spacing is 1 and each dab removes `alpha * (1 - weight)` where the weight is the hardness falloff — so this is a real erase, not the hard edge an earlier version of this record described.

### Magic Eraser Tool

`magic-eraser`

Erases every pixel similar to the one you click, to transparency, in a single click, bounded by Tolerance, Anti-alias and Contiguous.

The Magic Eraser is the Paint Bucket run in reverse: one click erases every pixel whose color falls within Tolerance of the pixel clicked, rather than a dragged tip erasing a stroke. It works like the Magic Wand without the preview, which is its whole cost — there is no marching ants, so the region it will remove is visible only in the History panel afterwards. Tolerance sets how far a color may differ and still count, Contiguous limits the erase to the region connected to the click rather than every match in the layer, Anti-alias smooths the boundary, and Opacity sets how completely the matched pixels are cleared. On a layer whose transparency is locked the matched pixels change to the background color instead of becoming transparent; on a Background layer Photoshop converts it to a normal layer first and then clears the matched pixels to transparency.

**Options bar**

| Control           | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | In this app                                                               |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tolerance         | A slider, 0 to 255. A low tolerance erases only pixels within a very narrow range of the clicked pixel; a high tolerance erases within a broader range. Adobe does not document a default; a widely-cited third-party value is 32. | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/MagicEraser.tsx:34` |
| Anti-alias        | A checkbox that smooths the edges of the erased area. On by default.                                                                                                                                                               | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/MagicEraser.tsx:80`   |
| Contiguous        | A checkbox. On (the default) erases only pixels contiguous to the one clicked; off erases every similar pixel in the layer.                                                                                                        | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/MagicEraser.tsx:38` |
| Sample All Layers | A checkbox. On samples the erased colors from the merged data of all visible layers rather than from the active layer alone.                                                                                                       | `missing`                                                                 |
| Opacity           | A label with a numeric field, 0 to 100 percent. Default 100. 100 erases the selected pixels completely; lower erases partially, leaving some of the color visible.                                                                 | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/MagicEraser.tsx:44` |

**Shortcuts**

- `Shift+E` — Cycles the slot shared with the Eraser and the Background Eraser. Adobe’s own help page prints the bare letter E beside the tool, but the tool does not have E to itself — the Eraser does.

**In this app:** `partial` — A working flood-based eraser: one click, one atomic commit, a hard 0–255 tolerance on Adobe’s scale rather than the Magic Wand’s 0–100, a default of 32 that matches the value third parties report as Adobe’s own, 4-connected Contiguous as a real 4-neighbor scan, and an Opacity that scales the alpha removed per pixel so a partial erase is a partial erase. It shares its args type with the Paint Bucket and both run the same mask code, which is why Contiguous and Tolerance are genuinely wired for both. Anti-alias is the finding: it renders with the app’s own legacy `Anti-aliased` spelling, which current Adobe pages have dropped in favour of `Anti-alias`, and with Photoshop’s real checked state, but the input carries `disabled` and the flood fill’s test is a hard threshold producing a boolean mask, so there is no coverage to anti-alias. Sample All Layers is absent, and the tool is structurally active-layer-only — `FillToolArea` reads the active layer’s own raster and refuses the Bedrock layer outright, so there is no merged data to sample. As in Photoshop there is no preview of the region about to be removed, and the app does not bind `Shift+E`: the eraser family shares one plain `E` registration with no Shift twin (`AppKeyboardShortcuts.tsx:483`), so the tool is selected only by cycling with Shift+B from the eraser slot rather than the cycle Photoshop uses. Its bar is the shared fill bar, built by `createFillToolbar` and rendered at `MagicEraser.tsx:24`.

### Paint Bucket Tool

`paint-bucket` · **G**

Fills the contiguous area of similar color you click with the foreground color or a pattern, in one click, at a chosen Mode and Opacity.

The Paint Bucket fills the whole connected region of similar color around the click in a single click. Tolerance decides how far a pixel’s color may differ from the clicked pixel and still be filled, Contiguous limits the fill to the region connected to the click rather than every match in the layer, Anti-alias smooths the boundary, and Fill chooses the foreground color or a pattern. Mode and Opacity composite the fill, so a fill is a real layer edit rather than a paste. It shares a Tools-panel slot with the Gradient tool. Unlike the Magic Eraser it fills rather than clears; and unlike the Color Replacement tool it is committed by the single click that starts it, with no drag gesture to continue or extend the region.

**Options bar**

| Control            | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                | In this app                                                               |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tool Preset Picker | The leftmost button on the bar, applying a whole saved options-bar state in one action.                                                                                                                  | `missing`                                                                 |
| Fill               | A dropdown choosing Foreground or Pattern; choosing Pattern enables a second dropdown from which a pattern is picked. Default Foreground.                                                                | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/PaintBucket.tsx:51` |
| Mode               | The blend mode for the fill, offering the 27 layer blend modes — Dissolve among them — plus Clear, the one extra this tool gets. Behind is the Brush's alone, so it is not offered here. Default Normal. | `missing`                                                                 |
| Opacity            | A label with a numeric field, 0 to 100 percent. Adobe states that lower values create more transparent fills. Default 100.                                                                               | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/MagicEraser.tsx:44` |
| Tolerance          | A slider, 0 to 255. Lower values such as 10 to 20 fill only similar colors; values of 100 or more fill a broader range. Adobe does not document a default; a widely-cited third-party value is 32.       | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/MagicEraser.tsx:34` |
| Anti-alias         | A checkbox that smooths the edges of the filled area. On by default.                                                                                                                                     | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/MagicEraser.tsx:80`   |
| Contiguous         | A checkbox. On (the default) fills only pixels contiguous to the click; off fills all similar pixels in the image.                                                                                       | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/MagicEraser/MagicEraser.tsx:38` |
| All Layers         | A checkbox. On fills based on the merged color data of all visible layers rather than the active layer alone, which is what lets the bucket fill an empty layer from the artwork beneath it.             | `missing`                                                                 |

**Shortcuts**

- `G` — Selects the Paint Bucket Tool; with the Gradient Tool active, Shift+G cycles back to it.

**In this app:** `partial` — One click, one atomic commit on the active layer, with the foreground color read off the live store at the moment of the click rather than mirrored into the args, and the fill composited as a real source-over so a 50 percent fill over transparent pixels is half coverage of clean red rather than half-black — that is the one place where this implementation is more correct than a naive lerp. Tolerance, Contiguous and Opacity are genuinely wired and share the fill code with the Magic Eraser. Four of the fill controls diverge. Pattern renders `disabled` under the real `Fill` label: there is no pattern registry, no tile and no processor branch that could read one, so it is present in the DOM and inert rather than absent. Anti-alias is the shared fill bar’s `disabled` checkbox, which carries the app’s own legacy `Anti-aliased` spelling and is inert for the same hard-threshold reason as the Magic Eraser’s. Mode is absent outright and cannot be added cheaply: the tool’s args type declares no blend mode, and the fill is applied to the active layer’s pixels rather than to a new layer, so a blend mode would be a per-pixel composite against a destination the processor does not address. All Layers is absent, and the tool reads only the active layer’s raster. As in Photoshop the commit is the click, with no drag gesture and no multi-region sequence.

### Clone Stamp Tool

`clone-stamp` · **S**

Copies pixels from an Alt-clicked source point and paints them under the cursor, in Aligned or Independent mode, with a soft or hard tip.

The Clone Stamp copies pixels from one part of an image and paints them into another. Alt-click (Option-click on macOS) sets the source point; release the modifier and drag to lay the copy down. Aligned, which is the default, fixes the offset at the displacement of the first stroke after the Alt-click and holds it for every later stroke, so a pattern continues across a series of strokes; with it off, every stroke restarts from the original sampling point, which is what makes repeatedly stamping one patch of clean skin work. Sample chooses whether the source is read from the active layer alone, from the active layer and those below it, or from all visible layers, and Ignore Adjustment Layers keeps adjustment layers out of a merged sample. The tool is a copy rather than a paint, so it carries the source’s own color and alpha and needs no foreground color at all. A stroke that overlaps the area it is copying from can read back what it has just laid down, which is why the documented technique when the source is close to the target is to clone a little, release, and start again.

**Modifiers**

- **Alt** — Click, at pointer-down, to set the clone source point. The decision is made at pointer-down, so a drag that began as a plain press keeps cloning even if the modifier is released mid-stroke, and a press that began with the modifier down never starts a stroke.

**Shortcuts**

- `S` — Selects the Clone Stamp Tool. Holding Shift while pressing it cycles the slot shared with the Pattern Stamp Tool.
- `[` — Decreases the brush size to the next smaller preset diameter. On the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, Color Replacement Tool, Smudge, Dodge, Burn and Clone Stamp.
- `]` — Increases the brush size to the next larger preset diameter. On the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, Color Replacement Tool, Smudge, Dodge, Burn and Clone Stamp.
- `0` — Sets the brush Opacity to 100 percent. On the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, Color Replacement Tool and Clone Stamp.
- `1` — Sets the brush Opacity to 10 percent. On the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, Color Replacement Tool and Clone Stamp.

**In this app:** `partial` — The most nearly complete of the seven, and the only one whose Alt gesture is implemented. Alt-click sets the source at pointer-down and paints nothing; the source and the stroke are both rebased into the active layer’s frame, which is safe precisely because the processor only ever uses their difference. With no source set the gesture is refused outright — not-allowed cursor, no stroke, no history entry — rather than accepted and committed as a no-op that would make undo appear to do nothing. The copy is a genuine copy: a soft-edged tip and a straight-alpha source-over per texel, carrying the source texel’s own alpha so a clone out of a transparent region leaves the destination transparent rather than painting it opaque black, with every read indexed into an immutable copy of the raster and every write into the buffer, so no dab can sample a texel a previous dab laid down. That read-back is taken once per stroke and not per dab for a second reason worth naming: the live preview re-runs the processor on every pointer move but always against the store’s own pre-stroke raster, never the previous frame’s preview, and the commit re-runs it once more over the whole path before publishing. Aligned is the one control that is wired and still diverges, and the divergence is worth stating precisely because the checkbox is real and the arithmetic beneath it is not Adobe’s. Adobe fixes the offset at the displacement of the first stroke after the Alt-click and holds it for every later stroke; the app recomputes the offset from the current gesture’s own first point on every invocation, so the offset is constant within a stroke — which matches — and re-anchors at the start of each new one, which is exactly the drift the mode exists to remove. Unaligned is not the other half of Adobe’s pair either: Adobe keeps the sampling point fixed at the Alt-click and moves only the destination, while the app measures from the gesture’s current end, so the read point slides backwards as the drag progresses. Both arms are one subtraction, so this is a missing anchor rather than a wrong formula, and the fix is a stored offset on the args rather than new pixel code. Size, Hardness and Opacity are all wired and the tip is borrowed from the shared brush engine, so a soft Clone edge is the same soft edge the other paint tools stamp. Ten of the thirteen controls are absent because the args type declares no field for any of them: Tool Preset Picker, Brush Preset Picker, Mode, Flow, Airbrush, both pressure toggles, Sample, Ignore Adjustment Layers, Brush Angle and the Clone Source panel. Ignore Adjustment Layers has nothing to ignore in this app even in principle — a layer source is blank, an image, a tool or an affine transform, and Levels, Color, Transform and Blur are destructive operations on a raster rather than layers sitting above a clone target. Mode is the one that would change visible behavior: the tool is a raster commit on the active layer, so a blend mode is a composite against the layer beneath and the one primitive here takes no mode. Size is capped at 500 px rather than 5000. The layer gate refuses the Bedrock layer and requires a source, and a previous version of this record added that it did not check the layer’s lock flag, so a locked layer would still accept a cloned stroke. That is no longer true, and the guard is central rather than local: `updateLayerByTool` returns early on an `isLayerLocked` layer (`useLayer.ts:334`) and so does `tempUpdateLayer` (`useLayer.ts:535`), which is the path the live preview and the source write both go through, so neither can reach a locked layer. What remains true is the narrower, verified fact: `layer.locked` is only ever set true by importing a PSD, and no panel in this app renders a lock control or a lock icon, so there is no in-app route to setting one.

## Focus and tone

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/focus.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/focus.notes.md).

### Blur Tool

`blur`

Paints blur under the brush, softening hard edges and reducing detail wherever you drag; the effect builds up pass by pass.

The Blur tool reduces local contrast and smooths detail in the areas you paint it over, so one pass is subtle and repeated passes are not. It shares a Tools-panel slot, a single options bar, and a tip with the Sharpen and Smudge tools: the bar carries a brush preset with its Size and Hardness, a Mode, a Strength percentage that seeds at 50% and which Adobe's own guidance says to keep low, and Sample All Layers, which is what makes the effect paintable onto a blank layer above the stack for non-destructive work. It is a different thing from Filter > Blur and from the Blur Gallery, which run a Gaussian, Box, Lens, Motion, Radial, Smart, Surface or Tilt-Shift, Iris or Field blur over a whole selection or layer in one command with no brush and no per-stroke build-up.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | In this app |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the blur is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. Photoshop exposes the whole preset library here; Size and Hardness are the preset's two live parameters, and a soft tip is what lets a stroke blend into its surroundings instead of standing out against them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `missing`   |
| Mode                | The blend mode the blurred result is composited with, rather than drawn at Normal, and a mode that shifts hue or saturation blurs the colour differently from one that does not. Third-party walkthroughs name Normal, Darken, Lighten, Hue, Saturation, Color and Luminosity as the choices, and one of them says the dropdown 'only offers a limited number of blends' - but no page states to what the list is restricted, and Adobe's current Blur page does not enumerate a Mode control at all.                                                                                                                 | `missing`   |
| Strength            | The percentage of the blurred result blended in per pass, 1-100% and 50% by default. It is the per-stroke build-up rate, not a radius: at 100% one pass is the full blur, and at a low value the same stroke has to be repeated to get there. Adobe and the CS-era documentation both describe 10-30% as the subtle setting and 50% or more as strong. The 1% floor is not Adobe's own statement - no Adobe page gives the range either way - but the CS2 Bible states it directly ("1 percent being the minimum and 100 percent being the maximum"), and a 2009 report on the tool repeats that the range is 1-100%. | `missing`   |
| Sample All Layers   | Off by default. With it on, the blur samples the composite of every visible layer, so painting on a blank layer above the stack produces a separable, opacity-adjustable result; with it off the tool reads only the active layer. The blur is written into whichever layer is active either way.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `missing`   |

**In this app:** `partial` — The app reaches the tool two different ways, and its options bar is the one that still falls short. Its options bar is a single Blur Radius slider plus an Undo Blur button; there is no brush, no Size, no Hardness, no Mode, no Strength and no Sample All Layers, because the bar's only argument is a radius in pixels that the processor hands straight to the canvas blur filter. It is also a paint tool, and the two forms are reached differently. Dragging on the canvas reaches `BlurToolArea`, which delegates to the shared `FocusToolArea`; a drag is committed as one undoable action, confined to a 40px round brush, and recorded as a raster-processor history entry rather than a filter. Moving the radius slider reaches the other form: the bar routes through `tempUpdateLayer` with no stroke points at all, so it still previews the WHOLE active layer, publishes no history entry, and is written later by the dirty-tool commit on tool switch, on export or in `mergeAllLayers`. So the brush exists but the bar cannot express it - there is no control that sets the tip's Size or Hardness, no Strength that governs how fast the effect builds up, no Mode and no Sample All Layers, and the radius that IS on the bar governs the whole-layer form only, never the painted one. A stroke therefore paints with a fixed 40px tip at the kernel floor whenever the radius reads 0. That makes it the closest thing this editor has to Filter > Blur > Gaussian Blur - a true Gaussian, with the canvas blur filter as its kernel - wearing Photoshop's Blur tool's name. The verdict is `partial` and not `placeholder` for one specific reason, and it is the same reason the Sharpen's is: the tool does reach the document. It commits a real blurred raster with a real history entry, and `placeholder` is defined as committing nothing. What it commits is simply not what Photoshop's tool commits, which is what `partial` is for. Every one of the four controls above is therefore absent rather than incomplete. `Flow` is not one of them: no page I opened puts it on the Blur bar, so it is omitted from the table as unsourced rather than recorded as a gap - and the app could not have rendered it in any case, having no per-dab and per-stroke opacity pair to express one with, so the omission costs no fidelity claim.

### Sharpen Tool

`sharpen`

Paints extra edge contrast where you drag, so a soft area reads sharper without sharpening the rest of the image at all.

The Sharpen tool increases local contrast at edges, and therefore the apparent sharpness, only in the areas you brush. It shares one options bar and one tip with the Blur and Smudge tools, and what separates it from the Blur is the direction of the local change: the Blur smooths, the Sharpen exaggerates the difference between neighbouring pixels over a wider radius, with a falloff that behaves like an unsharp mask rather than a flat average. Its bar carries a brush preset, a Mode, a Strength percentage, Sample All Layers and Protect Detail. It is not the Filter > Sharpen family: those are one-shot commands with no brush and no per-stroke build-up, and Sharpen More in particular is simply the Sharpen filter with a larger fixed amount and no controls of its own.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | In this app |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the sharpening is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. A small hard tip over one edge and a large soft tip over a whole face are two different jobs, and the tool has no other way to express that choice.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `missing`   |
| Mode                | The blend mode the sharpened result is composited with as you brush. On a dark edge Luminosity or Color keeps the sharpening from dragging the hue with it, which is why the mode is worth setting per area rather than once.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | `missing`   |
| Strength            | How much sharpening each pass contributes, 1-100% and 50% by default. It is a per-stroke build-up rate on a filtered copy of the pixels under the brush, not a kernel radius; the effect accumulates with repeated passes over the same place, and at 10-20% it is subtle where at 50% or more it degrades quickly. No Adobe page gives the range either way; the CS2 Bible states the floor directly ("1 percent being the minimum and 100 percent being the maximum") for the Blur and Sharpen Strength alike. | `missing`   |
| Protect Detail      | On by default, and on the current desktop bar rather than an Elements leftover. Adobe enumerates it there between Strength and Sample All Layers as "Select Protect Detail to minimize pixelation and maintain image quality" - the sharpening is what produces the pixelation and this is the checkbox that keeps it from doing so. The wording is the same one Adobe used for the Sharpen tool in Photoshop Elements, where it "ensures minimized pixelated artifacts while enhancing and sharpening".         | `missing`   |
| Sample All Layers   | Off by default. With it on, the tool sharpens using the composite of every visible layer, so on a blank layer above the stack the sharpening is a separable, opacity-adjustable layer rather than a destructive change to the pixels underneath.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | `missing`   |

**In this app:** `partial` — What the app's options bar ships under this name is the Filter > Sharpen > Unsharp Mask filter rather than the tool's own controls. The options bar is Amount (0-500%, 50% by default) and Radius (0-100 px, 1 px by default) - the Unsharp Mask's own control names, not the tool's - and there is no brush, no Strength, no Mode, no Sample All Layers and no Protect Detail. The Radius is the sharper divergence of the two, because Photoshop's tool has no radius control at all: the bar Adobe enumerates runs brush Size and Hardness, Strength, Protect Detail, Sample All Layers, and a write-up on the CS5 rebuild is explicit that 'the tool has no radius control, so it's really just for screen sharpening'. A slider the tool does not have is a control rendered in a place Photoshop has nothing, which is the same defect the Gradient's Opacity slider is filed under. It is also a paint tool, and the two forms are reached differently. Dragging on the canvas reaches `SharpenToolArea`, which delegates to the same shared `FocusToolArea` the Blur uses; a drag is committed as one undoable action, confined to a 40px round brush. Moving a slider reaches the other form: the bar routes through `tempUpdateLayer` with no stroke points at all, so the layer is previewed as a whole-layer convolution rather than committed by it, no history entry is written, and the entry comes later from the dirty-tool commit on tool switch, on export or in `mergeAllLayers`. The brush therefore exists, but neither the Amount nor the Radius on the bar reaches it - the stroke runs at the fixed 40px tip, and Photoshop's tool has no radius control at all, so the bar's Radius describes the filter form only. As on the Blur, the verdict is `partial` and not `placeholder` because the tool does reach the document: it commits a real convolved raster with a real history entry, and `placeholder` is defined as committing nothing. The kernel is a two-pass separable BOX blur subtracted from the source, which is an unsharp mask over a box kernel rather than over Photoshop's Gaussian; the file says so. That matters more for this tool than for the filter, because the addendum's own account of the three focus tools is that they are distinguished precisely by kernel behaviour - the Blur smooths, the Sharpen uses a wider radius with unsharp-like falloff rather than a box blur. The kernel class is not the gap here, because the app does have the box kernel and says so in caps. What is missing is Photoshop's Gaussian: a real unsharp mask subtracts a Gaussian-blurred copy, whose response decays smoothly away from an edge, while a box window responds flatly across its whole width and stops dead at the edge. At small radii the two are nearly interchangeable; at a wide one the app's Sharpen hardens a band of the full window width with a step at its boundary, where Photoshop tapers. So the Blur and the Sharpen here differ in radius and in magnitude, not in the shape of the kernel's response - which is exactly the distinction the addendum says separates them, and the app does not reproduce it. The one genuine strength here is over the pixels underneath: the blur runs on premultiplied colour with alpha unsharp-masked on its own scale, so a transparent hole does not bleed a ring into the opaque side - a halo Photoshop's own USM does not go out of its way to avoid either.

### Smudge Tool

`smudge`

Drags the pixels under the brush along the stroke, picking up colour where the stroke begins and pushing it where you pull.

The Smudge tool simulates a finger through wet paint: it picks up the colour where the stroke starts and pushes it in the direction you drag, blending what it carries into what it passes over. It is the only one of the three focus tools that transports rather than transforms, which is why it is the only one that needs Sample All Layers, the only one with Finger Painting, and the only one where sampling the wrong pixels shows up as a visible smear. Alongside the brush preset and Mode the bar has a Strength percentage - where 100% is described as effectively infinite, carrying one colour the whole length of the drag - plus Finger Painting, which starts each stroke with the foreground colour instead of the colour under the pointer.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | In this app                                                      |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the smudge is carried with, carrying its Size and Hardness. The smudge is the size of the fingertip, so the preset is a statement about scale rather than about texture.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Smudge/Smudge.tsx:138` |
| Mode                | The blend mode the carried colour is composited with; Adobe's own page for this tool puts "blend mode options" on the bar without naming a default, and Normal is the one every painting tool starts on. Darken and Lighten are the useful ones here: they smear only the pixels that are darker or lighter than the colour the stroke started on, which is how a smudge is used to push a background out from behind a subject.                                                                                                                                                                               | `missing`                                                        |
| Strength            | The percentage of the carried colour blended per dab, 1-100% and 50% by default. A Strength of 100% is described as equivalent to infinity: it carries the colour sampled at the start of the drag all the way to the release, at which point the smudge is effectively painting. Below 100% the carried colour fades and picks up the new colour under the brush as it goes. No Adobe page gives the range either way; the CS2 Bible covers the Smudge Strength in the same paragraph as the Blur and Sharpen one and gives the same floor ("1 percent being the minimum and 100 percent being the maximum"). | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Smudge/Smudge.tsx:168` |
| Finger Painting     | Off by default, and called "dipping" in older versions of Photoshop. With it on, the stroke first applies a drop of the foreground colour and blends it into the image, then smudges that through as if a finger had been dipped in paint; the Strength setting then specifies how much foreground colour is applied, so at 100% the Smudge becomes the Brush. With it off, the colour under the pointer at the start of the stroke is used instead.                                                                                                                                                           | `missing`                                                        |
| Sample All Layers   | Off by default, and called "Use All Layers" before CS2. With it on, the tool grabs colour from every visible layer and smudges it into the current layer. The layers underneath are not modified either way, which is what makes the recommended workflow - a new empty layer with the box ticked - non-destructive.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | `missing`                                                        |

**Modifiers**

- **Alt** — Reverses the Finger Painting setting for the length of the drag: if the box is off, Alt-dragging dips the tool into the foreground colour; if Finger Painting is on, Alt-dragging smudges normally.

**Shortcuts**

- `R` — Selects the Smudge tool, which is the tool that owns the R slot in the Focus flyout; Shift+R cycles to the Blur and the Sharpen.
- `[` — Decreases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.
- `]` — Increases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.

**In this app:** `partial` — This is the closest match in the family. The processor reads each covered pixel from the untouched source raster at the texel one dab-behind along the drag, never from the buffer it is writing, so colour travels exactly one segment per dab instead of compounding into a single streak; the falloff is the shared brush engine's tipAlphaAt, so the smudge's soft edge is the same edge the Brush, Eraser, Dodge, Burn and Clone Stamp stamp. Strength is a real per-dab coverage seeded at 50% as in Photoshop, and it is `partial` rather than `present` for one narrow reason: the bar lets the slider reach 0, where `SMUDGE_STRENGTH_MIN` is 0 and the module says so in caps, while every source that states a floor for this Strength puts it at 1%. The transport semantics are right, and the app matches Photoshop's layering rule without being told to: the stroke edits the active layer, which is exactly what Sample All Layers does not change. Three controls are missing rather than wrong. Mode has nowhere to live because no control anywhere in the app edits a layer's blend mode: `Layer.blendMode` is a data field the paint tool's own Mode select writes and the PSD importer sets, and a grep for `blendMode` across `src/components/` finds only that select - the Layers panel has no blend-mode control at all. Finger Painting needs an args field of its own before it can be a control, and it is a per-dab source selection rather than a setting on the same axis as the other three. Sample All Layers would need the composite, and the processor is handed one layer's bitmap. The Brush Preset Picker is partial rather than absent because this editor has one tip shape and no presets, though Size and Hardness - the preset's two live parameters - are both there. Alt is not bound to Finger Painting. There is no build-up while the button is held: the shared stroke hook appends a point to the drag on a pointer move and there is no timer and no dwell accumulation anywhere in it, so holding the brush still deposits nothing, and one stroke is one undo entry. That is the same absence this file calls the tool's defining interaction on the Dodge and the Burn, and it is why this tool is filed `partial` on the same bar rather than `implemented` - not because the drag misbehaves, which it does not, but because the interaction the tool exists for is not there.

### Gradient Tool

`gradient`

Fills a selection or layer with a gradient you define by dragging: the click sets the first colour stop, the release the second.

The Gradient tool fills the current layer, or the selection when there is one, with a smooth blend between two or more colours. Where you click is where the first stop sits and where you release is where the second sits, so the drag sets the length and the angle of the gradient at once, and the gradient clamps to its ends beyond the drag rather than fading to transparent - which is why a short drag fills everything. The bar runs from a tool-preset picker, past the Tool Mode dropdown, to the gradient swatch and then through the five gradient types, the Dither and Reverse checkboxes and a Method dropdown, and every one of those controls belongs to the tool itself rather than to a brush. A blend Mode, an Opacity and a Transparency checkbox are also part of the Gradient tool, but only on the older destructive Classic gradient: on the live tool they are layer properties in the Layers panel instead. From 24.5 the bar also offers that Tool Mode dropdown, which picks between the two, and the live gradient can be corrected after the fact by dragging its handles on the canvas.

**Options bar**

| Control                    | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | In this app                                                          |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tool Preset Picker         | The button at the left end of the bar, before everything else, which opens the drop-down of saved tool presets for the Gradient tool. Photoshop ships one - a "Circular Rainbow" - and it is the control every tool carries for recalling a saved bar configuration, so it is the bar's first stop rather than a Gradient-specific setting.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | `missing`                                                            |
| Tool Mode                  | The dropdown immediately to the right of the Tool Preset picker, picking between "Gradient" and "Classic gradient". It exists only in 24.5 and later, and it is not cosmetic: the choice changes which options follow it, since Mode, Opacity and Transparency belong to the Classic one alone. The classic tool is destructive and must be reapplied after Dither or Reverse changes; the live one writes an editable gradient adjustment layer instead.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | `missing`                                                            |
| Gradient preset picker     | The gradient swatch just to the right of the Tool Mode dropdown. Clicking it opens the Gradient Editor, where the stops, their locations, their colours, their opacity stops and their midpoints are edited and the preset saved; its dropdown arrow opens the presets library instead. It is two controls in one swatch, and the two do different things. On the live tool the Gradient Editor cannot be opened this way at all - the swatch is read-only there, and a live gradient is edited from its adjustment layer instead.                                                                                                                                                                                                | `missing`                                                            |
| Gradient Type              | Five buttons: Linear, a straight ramp from the start point to the end point; Radial, a circle from the start point at its centre to the end point at its outer edge; Angle, a sweep in the direction the drag points; Reflected, a linear ramp mirrored about the start point; and Diamond, a rhombus radiating from it. Linear is the default, and Angle, Reflected and Diamond are the three most often left off a smaller implementation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Gradient/Gradient.tsx:13`  |
| Mode                       | The blend mode the gradient is composited with, Normal by default, which is how a gradient is used to tint or to knock back whatever is beneath it rather than to replace it. It is a control of the Classic gradient only: on the live (default) Gradient tool there is no Mode in the bar at all, because the gradient is written as an adjustment layer and the blend mode is a property of that layer in the Layers panel instead.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | `missing`                                                            |
| Opacity                    | The opacity of the whole gradient, 0-100% and 100% by default. It scales the fill and is not a third stop: the gradient keeps its own alpha ramp, and this multiplies it. It is a control of the Classic gradient only - the teachucomp walkthrough is explicit that the Mode and Opacity drop-downs "do not appear in the Options bar Control panel if using the new Gradient Tool, as it applies its gradient adjustment in a separate adjustment layer", and on the live tool opacity is the adjustment layer's own property. So this row describes a control that is not on the 27.x bar for the default tool, and the app's status is partial because it renders a slider in a place Photoshop has moved the setting out of. | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Gradient/Gradient.tsx:129` |
| Dither                     | It adds noise at the boundaries of each colour in the interpolation so transitions appear smoother, which is what stops an 8-bit ramp from showing visible banding. On a live gradient the setting is live, so ticking it updates the existing gradient immediately; on the Classic tool it has to be reapplied. No Adobe page states a default for it, and a third-party walkthrough is the only one that calls it one, describing Dither-on and Perceptual as "both the default settings".                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `missing`                                                            |
| Transparency               | Enables the gradient pattern transparency. It is not available on the new Gradient tool at all - the checkbox belongs to the Classic gradient only - and with it off the opacity stops in the gradient are ignored.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `missing`                                                            |
| Reverse                    | Swaps the gradient ends, so the colour that was at the first stop moves to the second. As with Dither it is live on a live gradient and requires reapplying the gradient on the Classic tool, and as with Dither no page I opened states a default for it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | `missing`                                                            |
| Method                     | The interpolation method: Perceptual, which is the default and interpolates in the OKLab colour space so the ramp looks natural to the eye; Linear, which interpolates in linear colour space; and Classic, the interpolation Photoshop used for decades, kept for backwards compatibility. Perceptual became the default in 23.0, so gradients made in 22.x or earlier render differently in 23.0 and later unless this is set back to Classic.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | `missing`                                                            |
| On-canvas gradient handles | Not an options-bar control but the tool defining editing surface, and the load-bearing one. After the drag, two round handles mark the gradient ends and a small diamond between them sets the midpoint, all draggable straight on the canvas. Dragging a handle re-aims the gradient and changes its length; dragging the line itself - avoiding the dots and the diamond - moves the whole gradient rather than one end of it, and no modifier is involved. Photoshop added these on-canvas controls together with an automatic live preview in 24.5.                                                                                                                                                                           | `missing`                                                            |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the drag to multiples of 45 degrees, so a linear gradient lands on a square angle.

**Shortcuts**

- `G` — Reaches the Gradient tool, but only on the second press: a plain G selects the Paint Bucket, and it is Shift+G that cycles the pair. The Gradient tile declares no shortcut letter of its own, while the Paint Bucket's declares G.
- `Delete` — Removes the stop under the pointer from the on-canvas gradient line.

**In this app:** `partial` — The fill itself is right: the drag sets both endpoints, the projection clamps to the ends rather than fading to transparent, and a linear ramp puts the exact mean of the two stops at the midpoint of the axis. Everything around it is thinner than the bar. The bar has four controls where Photoshop's bar has eleven, and it does not even start where Photoshop's does: the Tool Preset picker is the control at the left end of the Photoshop bar and this bar opens with `Type` instead, so there is no saved-preset recall at all. Gradient Type offers only Linear and Radial - Angle, Reflected and Diamond have no representation in a fixed from/to pair. The Radial is also a different fill: the app's holds its end colour past the circle through the second stop, and no page I opened states that Photoshop mirrors there, so that difference is recorded as a structural consequence of the fixed `from`/`to` args rather than as a Photoshop behaviour. Dither, Reverse and the Method dropdown are all missing, and Method is the most consequential omission of the three: the app interpolates the two stops as plain per-channel RGB, which is closest to the Classic behaviour that Photoshop stopped defaulting to in 23.0, so every gradient this editor paints is one Method dropdown away from a different ramp. The Tool Mode dropdown is missing too, so there is no live/classic choice at all - the app is permanently the destructive one, and even a Dither checkbox would have had to be reapplied by hand. Transparency is absent, which happens to match the modern tool rather than the Classic one, but for the wrong reason: there is no alpha ramp at all. The Opacity slider is the one control the app carries that Photoshop has taken off the live tool's bar entirely - on the Classic gradient it is a bar dropdown, and on the live one it is the adjustment layer's own property in the Layers panel - so the app shows a control Photoshop moved, which is why that row is `partial` and not `present`. The preset picker and the Gradient Editor are gone, so there are no multi-stop gradients, no per-stop opacity or position, no midpoints, and no gradient styles. The two stops are two colour inputs in the bar rather than a picker, and they are the tool's only gradient state - there is no Foreground-to-Background preset and nothing to reset to. The load-bearing gap is the on-canvas handles: the tool area accepts the overlay context and never draws to it, and from/to are written only by the drag, so once the fill is committed its geometry cannot be changed at all without painting a second gradient over it. Photoshop's live-preview gradient, added in 24.5, is not a refinement of that - it is the difference between a fill and an editable object. Nothing is bound to Shift, so a drag is never constrained to a square angle. The two preset keys are bound nowhere in the app at all: `,` and `.` are on no keyboard handler, and `[` and `]` are registered but as the shared tip-size nudge, which is gated to the tools that carry a tip-size field and the Gradient is not one of them, so both are dead while this tool is active. The only `Delete` bindings belong to the two lasso tool areas, so no key removes a gradient stop. The bar's four controls are not the ones Photoshop sequences, so a user arriving from Photoshop finds neither the Order nor the Method. The verdict is `partial` and not `placeholder` because the fill does reach the document as a real raster with a real history entry; what it commits is not what Photoshop's tool commits, which is a narrower gradient with no editable object left behind.

### Dodge Tool

`dodge` · **O**

Lightens the tonal range you choose as you paint, the way holding back paper under a finger brightens a print.

The Dodge tool comes from the darkroom: a printer holds light back under a finger to lighten that part of the print, and this is the digital version. Dragging it lightens the pixels it passes over, and it keeps doing so for as long as the button is held, so the effect is built by dwelling rather than by painting more. It is a tone operation gated by a tonal range, which is what separates it from the Sponge tool in the same flyout - the Sponge is a chroma operation with a Saturate/Desaturate mode and neither a Range nor an Exposure. Exposure is the only intensity control on the bar: there is no Opacity and no Flow, unlike the paint tools. The bar also offers Airbrush, which makes the build-up automatic while the brush rests, and Protect Tones, which is on by default and keeps the lightening from shifting hue or clipping the ends of the range.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | In this app                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the dodge is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. A large soft tip with a low Exposure is how a dodge is built gradually; a small hard one is how a catchlight is placed.                                                                                                                                 | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:156` |
| Range               | Which tonal range the stroke is allowed to touch: Shadows, Midtones or Highlights, with Midtones as the default. Choosing the range is what makes the same tool usable on a face without taking the specular highlights with it, and it is why the Dodge and Burn are tone operations while the Sponge beside them is not. | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:126` |
| Exposure            | How strongly each pass lightens, as a percentage, 0-100% with 50% as the default, and the only intensity control on the bar. A low value with repeated passes is the intended workflow; a high one in a single pass is how a dodge turns into a blown highlight.                                                           | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:139` |
| Protect Tones       | On by default. A boolean that changes which pixels the stroke will touch: it helps maintain colour and prevents clipping in the highlights and shadows, which is the same work Adobe's older bar called Protect Skin Tone.                                                                                                 | `missing`                                                      |
| Airbrush            | Off by default. With it on, the effect keeps building on its own wherever the brush rests, without needing a new stroke - the automatic version of what holding the button still otherwise does, and the reason the tool is a "toning tool" that can build up "on the fly".                                                | `missing`                                                      |

**Shortcuts**

- `O` — Selects the Dodge tool; the letter is shared with the Burn and Sponge tools in the same flyout.
- `Shift+O` — Cycles through the tools that share the O shortcut, which reaches the Burn tool without leaving the canvas.
- `Shift+Alt+S` — Sets the stroke to the Shadows range while the Dodge tool is active, the same key the Sponge uses to desaturate. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+S on macOS.
- `Shift+Alt+M` — Sets the stroke to the Midtones range. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+M on macOS.
- `Shift+Alt+H` — Sets the stroke to the Highlights range. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+H on macOS.
- `0` — Sets Exposure to 100% while the Dodge tool is active, on the rule that any painting or editing tool takes a bare number for opacity, tolerance, strength or exposure.
- `[` — Decreases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.
- `]` — Increases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.

**In this app:** `partial` — Range and Exposure are both real and both wired: Range writes a field the processor reads, and Exposure drives a per-pixel amount rather than a display-only value, with the band's power driven by the exposure so a high value narrows the band instead of dragging a hard edge across the picture. The band itself is a quadratic falloff in Rec.709 luma of the encoded sRGB the editor stores, split at a flat luma 128. That is a defensible reading of what the tool does - Photoshop also scales stored channel values towards 255 - but it is a single hard split against a real tonal scale, and the three Photoshop bands are not equal halves of the range. The bar also matches Photoshop in a negative that is easy to get wrong: there is no Opacity and no Flow, only Exposure, which is why `DodgeBurnToolArgs` has no opacity or spacing field and takes both from the shared engine's defaults. Three controls are missing. There is no `Mode` control on the Dodge or Burn bar to be missing: the blend mode is fixed, and Peachpit's account of the tools is that they 'are effectively operating with the Color Burn and Color Dodge blending modes', which is why they shift colour and why Protect Tones has to be there to hold the colour back. Protect Tones is a real omission and the component says so: there is no field for it, so a checkbox would read as on while doing nothing. Airbrush is missing for the same reason. The Brush Preset Picker is partial rather than absent because Size and Hardness, the preset's two live parameters, are both present and clamped to 1-500 px and 0-100%. The largest behavioural gap is not a control: there is NO BUILD-UP. Each stroke commits once, at the slider's full Exposure value in a single pass, because a one-shot commit has to be a pure function of its args, which is also what makes the registry's replay reproduce it exactly. Holding the button still does nothing, so the tool's defining interaction is absent - and Airbrush, which exists precisely to make that build-up automatic when you cannot hold still, is missing for the same reason. Dodge and Burn deliberately share one options component, so a change to this control set cannot land on one tool and miss the other.

### Burn Tool

`burn`

Darkens the tonal range you choose as you paint, the way letting more light onto a print deepens its shadows.

The Burn tool is the Dodge tool measured from the other end: instead of holding light back, you let more of it onto the print, which deepens that part of the image. Dragging darkens the pixels it passes over, and it keeps darkening for as long as the button is held. Range confines the work to Shadows, Midtones or Highlights, and Exposure - the bar's only intensity control, with no Opacity and no Flow - sets how hard each pass works. Airbrush makes the build-up automatic while the brush rests, and Protect Tones is on by default and keeps the darkening from raising saturation or clipping the shadows and highlights.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | In this app                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the burn is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. A large soft tip with a low Exposure builds a burn gradually; a small hard one places a precise one.                                                                                               | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:156` |
| Range               | Which tonal range the stroke is allowed to touch: Shadows, Midtones or Highlights, with Midtones as the default. Restricting a burn to the shadows is what keeps it from muddying the midtones it was not aimed at.                                                  | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:126` |
| Exposure            | How strongly each pass darkens, as a percentage, 0-100% with 50% as the default, and the only intensity control on the bar. Low values with repeated passes are the intended workflow; a high one in a single pass closes the shadows up.                            | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:139` |
| Protect Tones       | On by default. A boolean that changes which pixels the stroke will touch: without it a burn raises the saturation of what it darkens as well as darkening it, and it can clip the ends of the range. This is the control Adobe's older bar called Protect Skin Tone. | `missing`                                                      |
| Airbrush            | Off by default. With it on, the darkening keeps building wherever the brush rests, without needing a new stroke.                                                                                                                                                     | `missing`                                                      |

**Shortcuts**

- `Shift+O` — Cycles from the Dodge tool to the Burn tool, which share the O shortcut; press it again to reach the Sponge tool.
- `Shift+Alt+S` — Sets the stroke to the Shadows range while the Burn tool is active. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+S on macOS.
- `Shift+Alt+M` — Sets the stroke to the Midtones range. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+M on macOS.
- `Shift+Alt+H` — Sets the stroke to the Highlights range. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+H on macOS.
- `[` — Decreases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.
- `]` — Increases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.

**In this app:** `partial` — The same processor as the Dodge, with the endpoint swapped: the burn's rule is c' = c - c * amount against the dodge's c' = c + (255 - c) * amount, and the module is explicit that burn is not the inverse of dodge. Range and Exposure are both wired to real per-pixel work through the same band function, and the band is a quadratic falloff in Rec.709 luma of the encoded sRGB the editor stores - a defensible reading, since Photoshop also scales stored channel values towards 0, but a single hard split at luma 128 where the three real tonal bands are not equal halves of the range. Protect Tones and Airbrush are both missing for the same reason as on the Dodge: `DodgeBurnToolArgs` has no field to hold them, and a control that renders a value the processor never reads is the failure this bar is written against. As on the Dodge there is no `Mode` control to miss, because the blend mode is fixed in Photoshop rather than selectable. The Brush Preset Picker is partial because Size and Hardness are present. The defining gap is again the absence of build-up while the button is held - one stroke, one commit, at the slider's full Exposure value in a single pass - which is a deliberate choice to keep the commit a pure function of its args so the registry replays it exactly, and which costs the tool the behaviour it exists for. This tool and the Dodge share one options component by design, so the control set cannot drift between them.
