### Sponge Tool

`sponge`

Raises or lowers the colour saturation under the brush, so a flat area gains colour or a loud one loses it, and the lightness underneath is untouched.

The Sponge tool subtly changes the colour saturation of an area. Saturate intensifies the colour's saturation and Desaturate dilutes it, and the tool reaches no further than that: it is the one brush in the toning flyout that acts on chroma rather than on tone, which is what separates it from the Dodge and the Burn beside it, and neither a Range nor an Exposure appears on its bar because neither means anything to a chroma operation. Flow is the bar's only intensity control, and where the Dodge and the Burn have neither Opacity nor Flow the Sponge has Flow and no Opacity, so the bare digit keys step Flow rather than Opacity. Dragging compounds: the effect builds up pass by pass and keeps building for as long as the button is held, which is why retouching with it is done at a low Flow with repeated passes. Adobe documents one more thing about it that belongs here rather than in the option table, because it is a rule rather than a control: when an image is in Grayscale mode the tool increases or decreases contrast by moving grey levels away from or toward the middle grey. Vibrance, the checkbox that sits beside Flow, is what keeps the Saturate direction from pushing an already-bright colour off the end of its range; it arrived with the CS4 rework of all three toning tools, which is the same release that gave the Dodge and the Burn Protect Tones.

**Options bar**

| Control               | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | In this app                                                      |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brush Preset Picker   | The tip the sponge is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. A large soft tip at a low Flow is how a whole area is evened out; a small hard one is how one stubborn patch is treated.                                                                                                                                                   | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Sponge/Sponge.tsx:172` |
| Mode                  | Saturate or Desaturate, and nothing else: Adobe names exactly the two, as 'Saturate: Intensifies the color's saturation' and 'Desaturate: Dilutes the color's saturation'. Which one is the default is not something Adobe states anywhere, so the app's own seeded value is recorded as a choice rather than as an Adobe fact.                | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Sponge/Sponge.tsx:133` |
| Flow                  | The rate at which the saturation changes, as a percentage, 1-100%, and the bar's only intensity control. Adobe describes it only as setting 'the rate of saturation change' and states neither a default nor a range; the 1% floor and the 50% seed are the CS2 Bible's and a third-party walkthrough's, not Adobe's.                          | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Sponge/Sponge.tsx:146` |
| Vibrance              | Adobe's only documented description of it is 'Select the Vibrance option to minimize clipping for fully saturated or desaturated colors', so it is a gamut guard rather than a second intensity control: with it on the stroke cannot push a channel off the end of its range. Whether Adobe ships it checked is not stated on any page found. | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Sponge/Sponge.tsx:163` |
| Airbrush              | Off by default. With it on, the saturation keeps building wherever the brush rests without needing a new stroke. It is listed in community descriptions of the bar rather than in Adobe own enumeration of it.                                                                                                                                 | `missing`                                                        |
| Use Pressure for Size | A pressure-tablet toggle that sizes the tip by how hard the stylus is pressed. No tool in this app reads tablet pressure, so the control would have nothing behind it.                                                                                                                                                                         | `missing`                                                        |

**Shortcuts**

- `O` — Selects the Dodge tool. Adobe lists the Dodge, the Burn and the Sponge as three rows with the same letter rather than one row, which puts the Dodge first; the Sponge is reached by cycling.
- `Shift+O` — Cycles from the Dodge tool to the Burn tool and on to the Sponge, which share the O shortcut.
- `Shift+Alt+D` — Sets the tool to Desaturate while the Sponge is active. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+D on macOS.
- `Shift+Alt+S` — Sets the tool to Saturate while the Sponge is active - and is Shadows on the Dodge and the Burn, on the same page of the same Adobe table, so the two tools share one key and Photoshop resolves it by which tool is selected. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+S on macOS.
- `[` — Decreases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.
- `]` — Increases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.

**In this app:** `partial` — This is filed partial on two independent grounds, and both are stated here rather than left for the next reader to infer. The first is the one the Dodge, the Burn and the Smudge already carry: there is no build-up. Photoshop's Sponge compounds for as long as the button is held and every tutorial retouches it at a low Flow with repeated passes, while this app commits once per stroke, on release, at the Flow value in full. That is what keeps the commit a pure function of its args, which is in turn what lets the registry's raster replay reproduce it exactly, and the cost is the tool's defining interaction - the same cost `docs/TOOLS-TOO-HARD.md` records for the other two toning tools. Flow therefore means 'the whole effect of one pass' here rather than Photoshop's 'the strength of one dab', and the two are only the same number at Flow 100. The second is the Vibrance checkbox: it is a control welded to one of its two states. It caps the chroma scale at the pixel's own gamut boundary, which is the strictest reading of Adobe's 'minimize clipping', and that cap can only ever bind in the Saturate direction - Desaturate moves every channel toward the pixel's own luma, so its result is the convex combination of two in-range values and provably cannot leave the range, which makes the checkbox do nothing in that mode. Airbrush and Use Pressure for Size are missing for the reasons given in the option table: the first is the build-up above and the second is a tablet this app does not read. Protect Texture and Tolerance are deliberately absent from this record's option table rather than filed as missing: no source puts Protect Texture on the Sponge's own bar (it is a Brush-panel checkbox) and none puts Tolerance on it at all - it belongs to the Magic Wand and the Color Replacement. Adobe's bare digit keys step Flow on this tool, because the Sponge has a Flow and no Opacity, and the app's Opacity table has no Sponge entry, so 0 and 1 do nothing here; that is recorded rather than listed, since the shortcut table describes Photoshop. Adobe's Grayscale-mode rule is also not implemented, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight: the rule pivots grey levels about mid-grey in a document MODE this app does not have, and on an RGB pixel with no chroma the chroma scale is already an exact no-op, so adding the pivot would make the tool behave the way Photoshop behaves in a mode that cannot be reached. Two seeded values are choices Adobe declines to document rather than divergences from it, and both are recorded in full at `SPONGE_MODE_DEFAULT` and `SPONGE_FLOW_DEFAULT`: no Adobe page states which Mode the bar opens on, and no Adobe page states a Flow default. The Mode seeds at Desaturate because it is the non-destructive direction - a saturated stroke that clips a channel cannot be painted back - and Flow at the midpoint of the range every other percentage control in this app uses. The pixel arithmetic is a chroma scale about a Rec.709 luma of the ENCODED sRGB the editor stores, in the same space and for the same stated reason as the Dodge and the Burn, rather than in a colour space Adobe names and this repo does not have; Adobe publishes no per-pixel specification for this tool, and the one community implementation that states its rule says the same thing. One deliberate departure from `computeLuma`: the pivot reads the stored channels and does not fold alpha in the way the shared helper does, because folding alpha composites a partly transparent pixel toward white and would drag its hue with it - the opposite of what a chroma tool should do to a cut-out edge. A fully transparent pixel is left alone outright. The stroke coverage field is the shared one, extracted out of `dodgeBurn.ts` into `src/util/stroke-coverage.ts` rather than written a second time, and dabs are unioned rather than summed so a replay cannot compound.

## Shapes

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/shape.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/shape.notes.md).

### Rectangle Tool

`rectangle` · **U**

Drag-defined rectangle or square with an optional corner radius, drawn as a shape layer, path, or filled pixels.

The Rectangle tool draws a four-sided figure from two drag corners, and Shift holds it square while Alt/Option draws it from its centre outward. Radius rounds the corners before you draw, and the shape it produces is a Live Shape whose four corner radii can afterwards be set independently — Alt/Option-drag the on-canvas radius control to break one corner out of the link. The separate Rounded Rectangle tool was removed in Photoshop 22.3 because the Radius field on this tool subsumes it. Clicking the canvas with no drag opens a Create Rectangle dialog so an exact width, height and corner radius can be typed instead of dragged.

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the drag to a square drag box, which is a square for the Rectangle tool and a circle for the Ellipse tool.
- **Alt** — Draws from the centre outward, so the press point is the middle of the shape rather than one corner.
- **Space** — Repositions the shape while the drag is still in progress, without changing its size.

**Shortcuts**

- `U` — Selects the shapes tool group. The five geometric figures share one app tool name and differ only by their figure, so U keeps whichever of them is active rather than forcing the rectangle; the Custom Shape tool carries its own tool name, and U from there lands on the rectangle. Nothing happens until an image is open.

**In this app:** `partial` — The drag geometry, Shift, Alt and the corner radius all behave as they do in Photoshop, and the radius is clamped to half the shorter side exactly as a rounded rectangle must be. That is the whole of what is right, and the divergences below are why the verdict is `partial` and not `implemented`. The three the group carries apply to the Rectangle verbatim: Path mode does not create a path, Pixels mode rasterizes onto a new layer exactly as Shape mode does rather than painting into the active one, and the options bar shares one colour with the rest of the app rather than carrying its own Fill and Stroke swatches, so the fill is whatever the global background colour currently is and there is no way to turn the stroke off at all. The Rectangle adds two divergences of its own, and the first is a default rather than a gap: it seeds a 5 px stroke where Photoshop seeds 1 px, so an untouched rectangle is drawn five times as heavy as Photoshop would draw it. The Radius slider runs 0–250 px with no numeric entry on the bar, and only the rectangle gets a radius — the app gates the whole control on this figure. Fill and Stroke are on the bar, then, and `partial` in the table above is the honest reading of them: what the app renders is a single wired `Filled` checkbox over its one shared colour, and it is the separate swatches with their None / Solid / Gradient / Pattern menu that are missing, not the controls. The mode group, the stroke width, the stroke type and the opacity each diverge from Photoshop’s control in the same way, and the path weight, the pixel-mode blend mode, the anti-alias control, the three path-operation rows and the gear are absent outright. A bare click is where this figure is at its closest: Adobe’s one documented sentence is this figure’s own, and all four of the fields it names — Width, Height, corner radii and align from centre — are in the app’s Create Rectangle dialog, so nothing is left over on this figure. The corner radius is seeded from the bar’s live slider and applied to the layer being created, so a radius typed in the dialog does not rewrite the slider behind the user’s back. What diverges is the entry point rather than the fields: `Shape W&H` is a control on Photoshop’s bar and this app’s bar has none, so here the exact geometry is reachable only by opening the dialog with a click.

### Ellipse Tool

`ellipse`

Drag-defined ellipse or circle drawn as a shape layer, a work path, or a filled pixel region.

The Ellipse tool inscribes an ellipse in the drag box; Shift holds it a circle, and Alt/Option draws it from its centre outward. It has no Corner Radius, because an ellipse has no corners, and the field does not appear in the bar. No desktop Adobe page enumerating the Ellipse tool’s bar was found, so that this matches Photoshop is a judgment rather than a documented match. The result is a Live Shape whose width, height and angle stay editable in the Properties panel. Clicking without dragging opens a Create Ellipse dialog for exact dimensions.

- **Alt** — Draws from the centre outward, so the press point is the middle of the shape rather than one corner.
- **Space** — Repositions the shape while the drag is still in progress, without changing its size.

**Shortcuts**

- `U` — Selects the shapes tool group. That is the whole of what is right, and the divergences below are why the verdict is `partial` and not `implemented`. The three the group carries apply to the Ellipse verbatim: Path mode does not create a path, Pixels mode rasterizes onto a new layer exactly as Shape mode does rather than painting into the active one, and the options bar shares one colour with the rest of the app rather than carrying its own Fill and Stroke swatches, so the fill is whatever the global background colour currently is and there is no way to turn the stroke off at all. The Ellipse then carries the same wrong default as every other figure, a 5 px stroke where Photoshop seeds 1 px, and keeps a cornerRadius: 0 key in its persisted defaults for a control its own bar withholds. Withholding Radius is the app’s rectangle-only gate, and that is a judgment about Photoshop rather than a documented match, since the only evidence for it is a third-party page and no desktop Adobe page enumerating the Ellipse tool’s bar was found. The bar itself is the shared one — the Ellipse gets no control of its own, so the options bar names it and shows the same controls every figure gets: the tool-mode select, the thickness slider, the Filled checkbox, the dashed toggle with its dash and gap sliders, the opacity slider and the live preview. That is the same set the rectangle has minus the radius, so the same reading applies to each: fill and stroke are on the bar as a wired Filled checkbox over one shared colour rather than as Photoshop’s two swatches, the mode group, the stroke type and the opacity each diverge from Photoshop’s control, and the path weight, the pixel-mode blend mode, the anti-alias control, the three path-operation rows and the gear are absent outright. A bare click opens the app’s Create Ellipse dialog, titled per figure, with Width, Height and From Center and no corner radius — the same gate as the bar’s, on a figure whose corners are not rounded anywhere on either side. Adobe’s own documentation of a click dialog is the rectangle’s, so this figure’s dialog is the app’s field set rather than a documented one.

### Line Tool

`line`

Drag-defined straight line or arrow, drawn as a shape layer, a work path, or a filled pixel region.

The Line tool drags a single straight segment between two points, and Shift snaps the segment to the nearest multiple of 45 degrees so it lands on a compass bearing. Its colour is the Stroke, not the Fill, because a line is an open path with a stroke and no interior to fill. The Arrowheads panel adds Start and End toggles, with Width, Length and Concavity to size them; Adobe documents it as a section of the Contextual Task Bar (Window > Contextual Task Bar), not a field in the options bar. The end caps are Butt, Round or Square.

The two things that are missing are the arrowheads and the shape of the bar. Arrowheads are absent outright — `drawShape` strokes a bare moveTo/lineTo pair, with no start or end cap geometry — which is why a line here can never become an arrow, and that is what keeps the verdict at `partial` rather than `implemented`: the tool that draws arrows does not draw them. The Cap select the app renders for this figure offers Photoshop’s three cap styles but only the Line figure gets one, where Photoshop offers caps for any stroked path, through the Stroke Options panel rather than a bar-level select. A bare click gets no dialog at all on this figure, and that is the contract rather than a gap: Adobe documents the Line tool as a drag and a release and never names a Create Line dialog, so the click refuses on the console instead of opening a dialog Adobe has not got. A line has no Width and Height on Adobe’s side either, so the drag is the only place either can give it a length.

### Triangle Tool

`triangle`

Drag-defined triangle with its apex at the top-centre of the drag box; hold Shift while dragging to constrain it to an equilateral triangle.

The Triangle tool, added in Photoshop 2021 (v22), draws a three-sided figure whose apex sits at the top-centre of the drag box and whose base spans its bottom. Adobe states the drag and the Shift constraint but never the resulting geometry, so reading that box as an isosceles triangle rather than a regular one is this description’s inference, not Adobe’s wording. Shift while dragging is the equilateral constraint — it forces the height to √3⁄2 of the width — and it is not a square-drag aspect snap. Alt/Option draws from the centre, and a single Radius control rounds all three corners together, because this tool has no per-corner radius handles. The tool is a shortcut for the Polygon tool at three sides, not a separate shape vocabulary.

Equilateral is absent outright, and it is the same gap the Shift row above reaches from the other direction. Corner Radius is withheld rather than absent: `drawShape` reads `cornerRadius` in its rectangle branch only, so a triangle field would take a value and round nothing, and this figure’s corners cannot be rounded here either way.

### Polygon Tool

`polygon`

Drag-defined polygon of any number of sides, with the side count set before the draw; the star of a given point count is a separate tool.

The Polygon tool is drag-defined, not a click-to-place-vertices tool: Adobe says to click and drag on the canvas, and the ordinary reading of that is a regular n-gon inscribed in the drag box — the regularity is this description’s inference, not Adobe’s wording. Sides sets the n before the draw and defaults to 5. The star is not this tool’s to draw in the current release: Adobe’s tools list puts a separate Star tool in the same shapes group, and the star attributes — the number of points, the Inner Radius that sets the depth of the indents and the Outer Radius that sets the length of the spikes — are documented on that tool, in the Contextual Task Bar and the Properties panel. Shift constrains proportions, Alt/Option draws from the centre — though a polygon is already centred in its drag box — and Control/Cmd while dragging rotates it. A single Radius control rounds every corner at once. The result is a Live Shape whose side count stays editable in the Properties panel.

### Custom Shape Tool

`custom-shape`

Draws a preset vector graphic from Photoshop's shape library, or one you define from a path.

The Custom Shape tool draws any of the vector presets in Photoshop’s shape library — a library that includes the Leaf Trees, Wild Animals, Boats and Flowers groups, with the full set reached through Legacy Shapes and More in the Shapes panel. Those four were the default loaded groups in a 2020 account, and Adobe Community threads from 2019–2021 report that the picker changed and moved them behind Legacy Shapes and More, so what a current install shows on first launch is not established here. Third-party accounts, not Adobe’s own documentation, say this is the only shape tool whose Shift constraint preserves the drawn shape’s own aspect ratio rather than squaring the drag box, so a recognisable graphic comes out undistorted. Its Path Operations menu is where the boolean work happens: New Shape Layer, Combine Shapes, Subtract Front Shape — which Adobe’s 2022 wording calls Subtract From Shape Area — Intersect Shape Areas, Exclude Overlapping Shapes, and Merge Shape Components, which converts the live shape into a plain path and warns you that it can no longer be edited component by component. No single Adobe page enumerates that whole set. Any path — drawn with the Pen tool, made from a shape layer, or produced by converting text to a path — becomes a new preset through Edit ▸ Define Custom Shape, and Preset Manager saves and loads the result as a `.csh` file.

The placeholder panel does list Photoshop’s real control names for this bar, so the six chips a user sees are the genuine Photoshop set rather than placeholders for placeholders: Tool Mode, Fill, Stroke, W/H, Shape Picker, Path Operations. That is why those six rows read `inert` and not `missing` — the names are on screen and nothing is wired behind any of them, which is the exact shape the `inert` status exists for. The three rows that were `partial` above are also `missing` rather than partial, but for the opposite reason: Stroke width, Stroke type and Opacity have no chip in this tool's list at all, and the real shape bar that carries them never renders here, because this tool is absent from the canvas dispatch that gives the other five figures their gesture surface. It is a `display: none` area, so the three modifiers named above — Shift, Alt and Space — are bound to nothing either, and the app’s Shift constraint, which squares the drag box for every figure except the line, has no drag to apply to. That is also the whole of the app side of the Shape W&H row: a bare click opens a Create <Figure> dialog on the five figures that mount `ShapeToolArea`, and this tool mounts `DummyToolArea` instead, so none of that runs here and a click with no drag does nothing rather than opening a sized dialog. Subtract needs a multi-subpath model with a fill rule, which a single convex outline cannot express, so the boolean operations are not a bar toggle away; they are a data-model decision first.

### Shape Tool (the Tools panel group; no entry by that name)

`shape`

Draws a vector shape, a path, or a filled pixel region, and stamps it onto its own shape layer.

Adobe’s Tools panel has no entry named “Shape Tool”, so there is no Photoshop tool behind this one: the panel groups seven separate tools — Rectangle, Ellipse, Triangle, Polygon, Star, Line and Custom Shape — behind a single group icon, and the Star arrived as a tool of its own in 26.10. Whichever of the seven is active, the three-button Mode group at the left of the options bar decides what a drag commits — a filled shape layer with a vector mask, a work path with no pixels at all, or a rasterized region painted straight into the active layer. Fill and Stroke are set independently of each other and of the drawing mode, so the same rectangle can be a solid block, a hairline outline, or an outline over a gradient. The drawn shape stays a Live Shape, so its fill, stroke, corner radius and dimensions remain editable from the Properties panel long after the drag.

**In this app:** `partial` — The largest gap in the group is a tool the app does not have at all: Photoshop’s shapes group is seven entries and this app’s fly-out is six — Rectangle, Ellipse, Line, Triangle, Polygon and Custom Shape (`toolbar-mapping.ts:128-135`) — so there is no Star here, and the `shape` registry entry this description hangs off is the group container rather than a tool the rail ever displays. The processor is live and every drag commits a layer, so nothing here is a placeholder, but the group diverges from Photoshop in three further ways worth naming. Path mode does not create a path: the mode only suppresses the fill inside the rasterizer, so a Path-mode shape still rasterizes to a layer with a stroke. Pixels mode is not a mode of its own: the figure is rasterized and put on a new layer exactly as in Shape mode, where Photoshop paints straight into the active layer and leaves nothing new in the Layers panel. And the options bar shares one colour with the rest of the app rather than carrying its own Fill and Stroke swatches, so the fill is whatever the global background colour currently is and there is no way to turn the stroke off at all. A click with no drag is the group’s one place where the app meets Adobe head-on: Adobe documents the click dialog in a single sentence, for the rectangle — "Click on the canvas to bring up the Create Rectangle dialog" — and the app opens a `CreateShapeDialog` modal for every figure except the Line, titled per figure, offering Width, Height and From Center, plus a Corner Radius field on the rectangle that is seeded from that figure’s live Radius slider and applied to the layer being created rather than to the bar. The click itself commits nothing: OK is the only commit, Cancel, the backdrop, the header × and Escape all close without one, and OK is disabled outright while a dimension is under 1 px. The Line is the exception and is excluded by contract rather than by taste — Adobe documents the drag and the release for it and never names a Create Line dialog, so a click there refuses on the console instead of inventing a dialog Adobe has not got. What the dialog still leaves out is per-figure rather than shared, and the triangle and polygon entries below each name their own figure’s gaps against what this renderer can honour.

## Pen and path

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/pen.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/pen.notes.md).

### Pen Tool

`pen` · **P**

Draws precise vector paths from click-placed anchor points, with draggable direction handles for the curves between them.

The Pen tool builds a path of straight and curved segments by clicking to place anchor points and dragging to pull out the direction handles that shape each curve. It draws no pixels: Path mode creates a work path in the Paths panel, which draws nothing on the canvas and can be stroked, filled or loaded as a selection later. The drawing mode group decides which of those you get — Shape makes a filled, stroked shape layer, Path makes the work path, Pixels rasterizes straight onto the current layer. Every path-construction decision the tool makes is a decision about vector geometry, which is why it stays sharp at any zoom and survives scaling that would blur a painted line.

**Options bar**

| Control                   | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | In this app                                                             |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mode                      | The three-button drawing-mode group at the left of the bar, and the control that decides what the rest of the bar shows. The current Pen settings page tabulates the values as Shape, Path and Pixels, and Adobe’s older drawing page names the same three buttons Shape Layers, Paths and Fill Pixels. Shape creates a shape layer with a vector mask; Path creates a work path that can be stroked or filled later; Pixels creates a rasterized shape directly on the current layer. The Fill, Stroke and Stroke width controls exist in Shape mode; the Operation, Path arrangement and Path alignment controls exist in Path mode. The app names this chip "Tool Mode". | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Fill                      | Fill color: a swatch that sets the color, pattern or gradient used to fill the shape, and can be set to None. Shape mode only. Double-clicking the swatch opens the color menu.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Stroke                    | Stroke color: a swatch setting the color of the shape outline, with a width and a stroke type (solid, dashed or dotted, with Inside/Center/Outside alignment, Butt/Round/Square caps and a corner treatment). Shape mode only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Operation                 | Path mode only. The path area option that decides how the component you are about to draw combines with the components already in the path: Add To Path Area, Subtract From Path Area, Intersect Path Areas, or Exclude Overlapping Path Areas. A shape tool may hold Shift to temporarily pick Add and Alt (Windows) or Option (macOS) to temporarily pick Subtract. The app labels this "Path Operations", and that is the single chip of that name in the list it renders — so this row, and not the Path Selection tool’s control below, is what the chip stands for.                                                                                                   | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Path Operations           | The Path Selection tool’s drop-down of the same four overlap modes, named Combine Shapes, Subtract From Shape Area, Intersect Shape Areas and Exclude Overlapping Shape Areas, plus Merge Shape Components, which fuses every overlapping component into one. It acts on an existing path component rather than on the one being drawn, so the Pen family shares the vocabulary without owning the control. The app’s bar does not carry it: the one "Path Operations" chip on it stands for the Pen’s own Operation control above, and nothing on the bar names this one — which is a divergence from Photoshop, not a rendering fact.                                     | `missing`                                                               |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the segment being placed to 45-degree angles.
- **Alt** — Converts a smooth point to a corner point when you click it, and unhinges a direction handle from its opposite so you can set the two independently while dragging a curve.
- **Ctrl/Command** — Temporarily activates the Direct Selection tool while you draw, so that you can adjust segments you have already drawn.

**Shortcuts**

- `P` — Selects the Pen tool, or keeps whichever Pen-family tool is already active — with the Freeform Pen or the Curvature Pen selected, P selects that one rather than jumping back to the Pen. Nothing happens until an image is open.
- `Shift+P` — Cycles through the tools nested in the Pen group.
- `Ctrl+Enter` — Loads the current path as a selection, the same as the Load path as a selection button at the bottom of the Paths panel.
- `Ctrl+Alt` — Activates the Convert Point tool temporarily while the Direct Selection tool is selected, when the pointer is over an anchor point.

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented. The processor exists but is the shared stub that returns a null bitmap, and its commit kind is unimplemented, so a drag over the canvas produces no layer, no history state and no durable operation. The app registers this tool, but it has no options bar of its own: the panel it renders is the shared amber placeholder with a TODO badge, and no control below is a working control — the ones that panel names are its chips, and the rest are absent from it entirely. The tool carries a single state key, its own name, so there is no setting behind any chip to be out of range. Selecting the tool changes nothing on the canvas — there is no path layer, no anchor point and no stroke to place. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. The app does bind the letter P and Shift+P cycling for the Pen group — and those two keys are the whole of the Pen's Photoshop chrome here, along with a tool-preset entry for the tool. Neither of the two shortcuts the bar above names that act on a path, `Ctrl+Enter` and `Ctrl+Alt`, is bound anywhere in the app. The options table above is the Shape and Path mode bar; Adobe's own enumeration of the Pixels-mode controls — `Mode`, `Opacity` and `Anti-alias` — carries the scope line "When using the Line tool or other shape tools", and the Pen settings page confirms that the Pen has a Pixels mode without ever listing what that mode's bar contains, so no row above describes Pixels mode and none is invented for it.

### Freeform Pen Tool

`freeform-pen`

Draws a path freehand, placing anchor points and fitting bezier handles to the stroke as you drag instead of clicking them one at a time.

The Freeform Pen takes a single drag and turns it into a path, so it is the tool for tracing something by hand rather than plotting it. The raw trail is simplified on release into as few anchor points as fit it, mixing straight corner points with curved ones. Turn on Magnetic and the trail stops following your hand and starts following the image: the live segment snaps to the strongest edge within Width, and fastening points are dropped along the border to anchor what you have already traced. It is the one Pen-family tool you can pick up in a photograph and use immediately, and the one to reach for when the precision of the standard Pen is more than the job needs.

### Curvature Pen Tool

`curvature-pen`

Draws smooth curved paths from plain clicks, computing the curve for you so there are no direction handles to manage at all.

The Curvature Pen is Illustrator’s Curvature tool ported into Photoshop, and it exists to remove the part of the standard Pen people find hardest. You click to place points; Photoshop fits the curve through them and keeps fitting as you add more, so a path is a sequence of smooth points and you never see, drag or think about a bezier handle. You shape it by pushing and pulling whole segments, and you switch one point between straight and curved with a double-click. Because the fit is continuous it will not give you the deliberately angular corner the standard Pen can, nor the deliberately flat run of a long handle; it is for the organic outline, and the standard Pen for everything else. It arrived in Photoshop CC 2018 (19.0) and is the newest tool in this family.

| Path thickness (Weight)   | The gear icon in the options bar opens the Path Options flyout, where the width and color of the on-canvas line representing the path are set. ### Add Anchor Point Tool

`add-anchor-point`

Inserts an anchor point into an existing path exactly where you click on a segment.

The Add Anchor Point tool subdivides a path. It only means anything against a path that already exists and is selected in the Paths panel, which is why it is a Tools-panel entry rather than a mode of the Pen: the standard Pen reaches the same result on its own when Auto Add/Delete is on, and this tool is the explicit version for when you want to add a point without switching tools mid-drag. Clicking a segment inserts a point there; dragging while you click reshapes the path as you add, so you can bend the line and place the new point in one gesture. The point it adds is a smooth point with direction handles, which is why the segments either side of it can change shape rather than merely being cut in two.

_Photoshop gives this tool no options bar of its own._

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented. Photoshop documents no options-bar control specific to this tool — selecting it shows the Pen group's bar, so every control on it belongs to the Pen and none is the Add Anchor Point tool's own — which is why its options table is empty. What the app does render is the standard Pen's chip list, on a panel with a TODO badge, over a tool whose registered processor is the same shared stub that returns a null bitmap the whole Pen family uses, over state that is nothing but its own name, and over no Paths panel to select a path in. The app's SidebarLeft gives this tool the same pen-nib icon as the Pen itself, so the three anchor-point tools are visually indistinguishable from it. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. The keyboard is the other half of the gap. The app binds exactly two keys for this family: `P`, which selects the Pen tool or keeps whichever of the three pens is already active, and `Shift+P`, which cycles that same three. The rail’s Pen flyout lists six tools, so the cycle covers three of the six and the three path-modification tools — Add Anchor Point, Delete Anchor Point and Convert Point — are unreachable from any key in the app.

### Delete Anchor Point Tool

`delete-anchor-point`

Removes the anchor point you click from an existing path, and the two segments around it re-solve.

The Delete Anchor Point tool takes a point out of a path that already exists and is selected in the Paths panel. The consequence is the interesting part: the two segments that met at the removed point do not simply join end to end, they are re-fitted across the new span, so deleting a point from a curve usually changes the curve and can smooth out the kink that point was holding. It is the counterpart to the Add Anchor Point tool and, like it, mostly exists so the Pen family is not a three-tool round trip for every edit; the standard Pen reaches it on its own when Auto Add/Delete is on. Note the trap Adobe calls out: the keyboard Delete key is not this tool. It removes the point and the segments joined to it, splitting the path in two.

_Photoshop gives this tool no options bar of its own._

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented. Photoshop documents no options-bar control specific to this tool — selecting it shows the Pen group's bar, so every control on it belongs to the Pen and none is the Delete Anchor Point tool's own — which is why its options table is empty. What the app does render is the standard Pen's chip list, on a panel with a TODO badge, over a tool whose registered processor is the same shared stub that returns a null bitmap the whole Pen family uses, over state that is nothing but its own name, and over no Paths panel to select a path in. The app's SidebarLeft gives this tool the same pen-nib icon as the Pen itself. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. The keyboard is the other half of the gap. The app binds exactly two keys for this family: `P`, which selects the Pen tool or keeps whichever of the three pens is already active, and `Shift+P`, which cycles that same three. The rail’s Pen flyout lists six tools, so the cycle covers three of the six and the three path-modification tools — Add Anchor Point, Delete Anchor Point and Convert Point — are unreachable from any key in the app.

### Convert Point Tool

`convert-point`

Converts an anchor point between corner and smooth, with or without independent direction lines.

The Convert Point tool changes the type of a point on a path that already exists and is selected in the Paths panel, and a single drag does three different things depending on what you grabbed. Drag away from a corner point and direction lines appear, making it a smooth point whose handles you then shape. Click a smooth point and it becomes a corner point with no direction lines, so the segments either side leave it independently. Drag one of a smooth point’s direction points and the point stays smooth but the two handles are unhinged, so they can point in different directions — which is what produces an S-curve. The Pen reaches all three with Alt held, and with the Direct Selection tool selected, Ctrl+Alt (Windows) or Command+Option (macOS) over an anchor point reaches this tool without leaving that tool.

_Photoshop gives this tool no options bar of its own._

**Shortcuts**

- `Ctrl+Alt` — Activates the Convert Point tool temporarily while the Direct Selection tool is selected and the pointer is over an anchor point.

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented. Photoshop documents no options-bar control specific to this tool — selecting it shows the Pen group's bar, so every control on it belongs to the Pen and none is the Convert Point tool's own — which is why its options table is empty. What the app does render is the standard Pen's chip list, on a panel with a TODO badge, over a tool whose registered processor is that same shared null-bitmap stub and over state that is nothing but its own name. This is also one of the tools the durable document refuses: converting a history item that names it is rejected as an unsupported feature rather than silently replayed. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. `Ctrl+Alt` is named above as the way to reach this tool from the Direct Selection tool, and the app registers no Alt-bearing keybinding at all: the five tools that read `altKey` are the shape tool, the elliptical marquee, the eyedropper, the clone stamp and the magnetic lasso, none of which is in this family. The keyboard is the other half of the gap. The app binds exactly two keys for this family: `P`, which selects the Pen tool or keeps whichever of the three pens is already active, and `Shift+P`, which cycles that same three. The rail’s Pen flyout lists six tools, so the cycle covers three of the six and the three path-modification tools — Add Anchor Point, Delete Anchor Point and Convert Point — are unreachable from any key in the app.

## Type and crop

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/type-crop.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/type-crop.notes.md).

### Crop Tool

`crop` · **C**

Frames a new boundary for the photo; nothing is committed until you confirm, and Esc restores the old framing.

A crop sets a new boundary for the document. Selecting the Crop tool shows a crop box you can drag out and resize by its handles; dragging just outside a corner rotates the image inside the box, which is Adobe's own sentence — "Place the pointer a little outside the corner handles and drag to rotate the image. A grid displays inside the crop box and the image rotates behind it" — while dragging inside the box moves the image and leaves the box where it is. Adobe's newer crop page says the opposite on both counts ("hover outside a corner to rotate the crop box … To move the crop box, drag it from inside"), and the two Adobe pages cannot both describe the shipping tool; the behaviour asserted here is the one two Adobe pages and the third-party literature agree on. Nothing is committed until you confirm with Enter (Windows), Return (Mac OS), the Done button or a double-click inside the box, and Esc cancels and restores the framing you had before. Photoshop treats the crop as non-destructive until that commit, and it is only irreversible once the commit happens with Delete Cropped Pixels on. This describes Photoshop 2024-2026, where Straight Crop is the tool's default mode and Perspective Crop is a separate tool in the same flyout rather than a mode of this one.

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Two different things, both Adobe's. Dragging a fresh box with it held constrains that box to a square; dragging a corner handle with it held constrains the proportions the box already has.
- **Alt** — Draws the crop box outward from its center, so the opposite edge moves as well.
- **Alt+Shift** — Constrains the proportions and draws from the center at the same time.
- **Ctrl / ⌘** — Two more of Adobe's: held on its own it invokes the Straighten tool without visiting the bar, and held during a drag it temporarily disables snapping to the crop box edge.
- **Shift while rotating** — Restricts the rotation to 15-degree increments.
- **Ctrl while rotating** — Prevents the crop box from shrinking as it rotates.

**Shortcuts**

- `C` — Select the Crop tool.
- `Shift+C` — Re-selects the same tool rather than cycling a flyout. Adobe groups four tools on `C` — Perspective Crop, Slice and Slice Select beside the Straight Crop this record describes — and this tile holds one entry, so the other three are unreachable.
- `Enter / Return` — Commits the pending crop, the same as the Apply button.
- `Esc` — Cancels the pending crop and restores the previous framing.
- `X` — Switches the crop box orientation between portrait and landscape. Unbound in the app.
- `O` — Cycles the overlay options. Unbound in the app — `O` selects the Dodge tool.
- `Shift+O` — Cycles the orientation of the asymmetric overlays. Unbound in the app — `Shift+O` selects the Burn tool.
- `Backspace / Delete` — Resets the crop box. Unbound in the app for this tool.

**In this app:** `partial` — The app's crop edits the document frame rather than a tool layer, and it is not a raster commit at all. The crop's processor is declared with `commit: 'document-operation'`, and that commit kind is refused by every layer path — painting on it, replaying it into a layer and converting it to a durable layer all bail out — so the raster trim in src/tools/crop.ts is declared and unreachable: what actually commits is applyDocumentCrop, which takes the rect unclamped, converts it into the next documentFrame and dispatches a COMMIT_DOCUMENT_EDIT carrying a SET_DOCUMENT_FRAME_ACTION history entry with the previous frame. The frame changes at once — smaller or larger, depending on the rect — and everything outside the new frame stops rendering, while layer positions and sources are untouched, so the discarded pixels are still held in the layer bitmaps and undo puts the frame back. That is Photoshop's Delete Cropped Pixels OFF case — the canvas shrinks, the pixels are kept — not the ON case, which permanently removes them. What the app genuinely lacks is the setting itself, which it can neither offer nor invert, and the Image > Reveal All menu item, which does not exist anywhere in the app. The rect may be dragged past the image edge, and the commit follows it there: applyDocumentCrop normalises the rect with sortRoundRect, which sorts and rounds each edge once without the clamp trimRect applies, so a rect reaching past an edge commits a larger documentFrame and a rect reaching before the origin anchors the frame negatively. The commit dispatches no fill of any kind and touches no layer, so the band the growth adds is covered by no layer and stays transparent whatever the bottom layer is — that is OVR-1 in docs/OVERRIDES.md, recorded by hand, and it is the decision for Photoshop's Background-layer case rather than an omission of the fill. Nothing else in the stack caps a frame: the one limit is in applyDocumentCrop itself, which refuses anything past the 4096px per side or the 16777216px area — that is, anything outside a 4096 x 4096 box, with the per-side arm subsuming the area arm because 4096 x 4096 IS the area ceiling. The reason is not the largest canvas a browser can allocate; it is iOS Safari's ceiling and its failure mode. Safari's maximum canvas AREA is 16777216 and it fails there SILENTLY: getContext('2d') still hands back a context and every draw becomes a no-op, so an over-area document renders blank with no exception to catch, and this app ships mobile surfaces. 2^24 is also the lowest of the ceilings the browsers it targets impose, which is what makes it the one value that is correct everywhere at once. The per-side figure is derived from that area ceiling rather than from any browser constant, because an area ceiling bounds how many PIXELS a surface holds and says nothing about its longest edge, and a crop rect can be dragged arbitrarily far past an edge at low zoom. Photoshop's two synthesising values, Content-Aware Fill and Generative Expand, are absent from the app for reasons that are not about the crop, and the crop's bar renders no Fill control at all. Dragging inside the crop box translates the rect rather than picking up the layer under the pointer, because CropToolArea never passes one and so the branch that would move the image never runs; whether that is a divergence is not settled, because Adobe's current crop page says an inside drag moves the box. The pending rect is not written through to the persisted settings — the crop arm of the settings saver omits the rect and the pre-ratio rect before persisting — so the aspect ratio survives a tool switch and the draft does not, and switching away from the Crop tool and back discards the draft. That is closer to Photoshop's cancel-on-Escape than to its commit-on-switch. On modifiers, the fresh-drag half of the Shift, Alt and Alt+Shift rows above is implemented: CropToolArea passes `constrainToSquare` and `fromCentre`, the same pair RectangularSelectionToolArea passes, `sampleFreshDragModifiers` reads `shiftKey` and `altKey` per pointer event rather than once at press time, and `adjustFreshPoint` takes the square on the RADIUS per axis before mirroring the drag, so Alt+Shift is a square centred on the press point rather than one that has drifted off it. Shift outranks the bar's Ratio while it is held, and a fresh drag with neither key still obeys that Ratio. Command and Control are deliberately NOT the aspect modifier on a fresh drag: `getEdgeAtPoint` captures a box's own ratio only for a press that landed ON that box, so neither key reaches the geometry of a new box at all, which is Adobe's arrangement — Command is the crop's Straighten and edge-snap key and constrains no marquee's proportions. Two residues are left. The capture on a HANDLE resize still honours Control and Command as well as Shift, where Adobe gives them no proportion lock; it is the hook's one shared answer to that row and the Move tool, the text tool and the marquees all read it. And Alt on a handle RESIZE does not resize from the centre, so the Alt row is implemented for a new box and not for an existing one. The Ctrl, Shift-rotate and Ctrl-rotate rows remain aspirational. Enter and Esc are the exception to that pattern: CropToolArea installs its own window keydown listener rather than a table entry, so Enter commits and Esc cancels for real, and neither is reachable from the shared keyboard table. The panel's own two buttons are the same two actions under different names: Adobe calls the pair Done and Cancel, this app calls them Apply and Clear, and both are greyed until a real box is drawn, so a bare click commits nothing. What Photoshop's pair adds and this one does not is the commit by double-clicking inside the box, which has no handler anywhere in the crop path — `applyDocumentCrop` has exactly two callers, the window-keydown Enter in CropToolArea and the panel's own Apply, so there is no third route a double-click could arrive by, and neither CropToolArea, useRect, document-gesture nor the panel reads a dblclick, an onDoubleClick or a click detail. X is unbound, and O and Shift+O are actively harmful to repeat: O selects the first of the three-tool tonal group, and Shift+O cycles it, so a second press lands on Burn and a third on Sponge — a three-step cycle over Dodge, Burn and Sponge, not a two-tool toggle. The crop tile holds a single entry, so Shift+C re-selects the Crop tool rather than cycling a flyout, and Perspective Crop, Slice and Slice Select are not in the tool registry at all.

### Horizontal Type Tool

`text` · **T**

Sets a typed string into the document as a raster text layer, with font, size, leading, tracking and caps controls.

Photoshop's Type tools create live, vector-based type: glyph outlines re-rendered from the font, so a type layer stays resolution-independent and editable until you deliberately rasterize it. Clicking places point type, whose lines are independent and never wrap; dragging a bounding box places paragraph type, whose lines wrap and reflow as you resize the box. Type can also flow along an open or closed work path, or fill the inside of a closed shape. Paragraph settings — alignment, justification, indents and hyphenation — apply to paragraph type only, because with point type each line is its own paragraph. The anti-aliasing pull-down — None, Sharp, Crisp, Strong and Smooth, Sharp by default — is no longer on the type options bar. The five presets themselves are unchanged and are reached from the Character panel, the layer's properties and the Type menu instead; Adobe's own help still lists the type options bar among the four places characters can be formatted, without naming anti-aliasing there. When the pull-down came off the bar is community-reported only — an Adobe Community report of August 2025 puts it at Photoshop 26.10 — and is not asserted here.

**Shortcuts**

- `T` — Select the Type tool.
- `Shift+T` — Re-selects the same tool rather than cycling a flyout. Adobe groups four tools on `T` — Horizontal Type, Vertical Type, Horizontal Type Mask and Vertical Type Mask — and this tile holds one entry, so two of the four are unreachable and the other two are one keypress away on a different tile that does not exist.

**In this app:** `partial` — The app's type layer is baked pixels, not live type. renderText paints the string into a 2D context with fillText, and the text creator hands back a single OffscreenCanvas, so what reaches the Layers panel is a bitmap. On the runtime path the layer renderer re-runs a tool's creator only for the six shape tools and text is not among them, so the visible canvas, undo replay and the PSD writer all draw `layer.bitmap` and enlarging a text layer rescales those pixels where a Photoshop type layer re-renders at the new size. The durable path is the exception and the runtime claim is not the whole truth: the durable materializer re-runs the text creator from the retained args, so the characters survive in one of the two engines and are re-derivable there. There are now two kinds of type layer, `kind: 'point' | 'paragraph'`, and the gesture that placed the draft picks one: a press whose pointer travelled no more than 3 CSS px on either axis places point type, anything further places paragraph type. Adobe distinguishes the two by intent — click the canvas and start typing for point text, drag out a box and type inside it for paragraph text — and documents no threshold, no minimum box size and nothing about which way a box grows, so all three are this app's own, as is measuring the travel on both axes rather than one. The threshold is applied by the Text tool, and NOT by `useRect`, which has no movement check of its own because it is also the crop's, the move's and every selection tool's. It is measured on the POINTER's travel in client px, which is the unit the threshold is defined in: the rect `useRect` hands back is document px, already divided by the contain fit, so reading the threshold off its extent put it in the wrong units — 3 document px is 2.92 screen px on an 800x600 document and 0.58 on a 4000x3000 one. `useRect` additionally exposes which element the press hit, so a press inside an existing draft or on one of its handles is a move or a resize and cannot change what kind of box the draft is; before that, any press on a draft larger than the threshold silently reclassified it, because a box holding text is always wider than 3px. A paragraph box has real authority over its text: its width is the width the user dragged, clamped to the document before anything is measured, the lines wrap inside that width greedily at spaces, and only the height is derived from the content — `calculateNewRect` grows a paragraph box downward and never grows or re-places its width, while a point box still grows to the widest line and is still re-placed by the alignment arm. Breaking happens at spaces only, and a word too wide for the box overflows rather than being broken or hyphenated, which is this app's reconstruction of Adobe's off-by-default hyphenation and not a documented behaviour. A newline is a hard break in both kinds. The draft overlay draws Adobe's overflow indicator while the text outgrows the box — "a small box or circle containing a plus symbol (+) appears in place of a handle in the corner of the boundary" — and its 8 px size, its bottom-right corner and its colour are this app's; it is box chrome rather than ink, so the creator never draws it and a committed layer carries no icon. `kind` is deliberately kept out of the persisted settings, so a remembered paragraph cannot wrap the next draft inside the last layer's box before the user has dragged anything, and a settings record written before the field existed resolves to point type — the only thing this app could draw before this revision. Text is typed onto the CANVAS, not into a field: a transparent contenteditable overlay is laid over the type box, so the caret, the insertion point and the character selection are the browser's own, and a fresh box arrives holding `Lorem ipsum` already selected so the first keystroke replaces it. Commit and Cancel appear only while a box is open, which is the state Adobe documents as edit mode. Escape and Ctrl/Cmd+Enter commit, a click elsewhere commits and then places the next box, and the commit still creates a raster layer. What the caret does not buy is per-character formatting: one flat `TextToolArgs` still holds a single face, size and colour for every character. The colour row is the one this file used to get backwards. There IS a colour control — a native colour input, `Text.tsx`'s `#text-color`, that writes through to the args and from there into renderText — and it is the tool's own setting: the bar no longer mirrors the global foreground swatch into the args on every render, which is what the earlier text claimed. What the app still lacks is Photoshop's Color Picker rather than the platform's, the Alt+Backspace and Ctrl+Backspace foreground/background bindings (the keyboard table registers two `alt: true` bindings, for the sponge tool's two mode steps, so the binding mechanism is not the obstacle — the type tool has no alt-bearing action to bind), per-character scoping, and Photoshop's default of seeding the type colour from the foreground swatch — the app's seed is a fixed black. Font size is now a number field over Adobe's `CharacterStyle.size` range of 0.01-1296, which holds the user's own string while it is being typed and clamps at the commit rather than on every keystroke, and it accepts NO unit suffix at all — the value goes straight into `Number()` and into a px shorthand, where Adobe's six-unit field is not reproduced. The unit is CSS px rather than points because the canvas carries no document resolution, so a point has no denominator here. Its `step` is `any`: a `min` of 0.01 carrying an integer step would put the landable values on a 0.01, 1.01, 2.01 grid, which leaves the seeded 64 off-grid on first paint and Adobe's own 1296 unreachable by the spinner. The font list is still fourteen hard-coded families rather than the system enumeration, and there is no Font Style combo box at all — the Bold and Italic buttons are booleans, not a list of the family's own styles, so a family-specific weight like Semibold or Condensed is unreachable and the two toggles cannot express a faux style the way Photoshop synthesizes one for a family that lacks a weight. Leading is still a unitless multiplier of the font size rather than an absolute baseline-to-baseline distance, but its default is now 1.2, which is Adobe's auto-leading figure — `JustificationProperties.autoLeadingAmount` defaults to 120, the percentage of type size used for auto leading — so the number matches Photoshop's default and the semantics behind it do not. Tracking arrived as a slider over -1000..1000 in 1/1000 em, applied as `ctx.letterSpacing` where the platform has it and as a hand-placed per-grapheme advance where it does not, and that fallback drops kerning and ligatures across the cluster boundaries it measures. All Caps and Small Caps arrived through `ctx.fontVariantCaps`, assigned after `ctx.font` because assigning the font resets it, and the small-caps value synthesises where the family has no real small caps, which is Adobe's own documented rule. Underline and Strikethrough arrived as two more booleans drawn in the type colour, which is the whole of what Adobe documents about them: its `Underline` enum is `NONE / LEFTINVERTICAL / RIGHTINVERTICAL` with no style, weight, offset or colour of its own, and the Underline Options dialog is InDesign's. Two figures in that pair are this app's own and not Adobe's: the rule sits 0.1em below the baseline, which no Adobe page states, and its thickness is `max(1, round(fontSize / 16))`, which Adobe does not document at all. Rendering moved to `textBaseline = 'alphabetic'` with the baseline placed from the measured `fontBoundingBoxAscent`, because `'top'` is a font-dependent offset that matches no exposed metric. Font size is the unit that diverges, not the range. T is the only type key, and only while the caret is not in the editor — a contenteditable target counts as a field, so a shortcut that does not opt into inputs is refused while the overlay holds focus, and a T pressed mid-edit types a letter rather than reselecting the tool. The type tile holds a single entry, so Shift+T re-selects the same tool instead of cycling a flyout — and that one entry stands in for a four-tool group.

## Move, transform and adjustments

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/transform.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/transform.notes.md).

### Move Tool

`reposition` · **V**

Photoshop's Move tool (V) drags layers, selections and artboards around the document, and hosts the transform box Free Transform hangs off.

The Move tool is how content gets placed. Select it, press on a layer, a selection or an artboard, and drag: the layer follows the pointer and settles when the button comes up, so a single drag is a single undo step. It is also the entry point to everything geometric — with Show Transform Controls checked, the same bounding box appears and dragging its handles scales, skews and rotates the layer, which is exactly the state Cmd+T enters. Auto-Select makes the tool pick the layer under the pointer instead of requiring a trip to the Layers panel, and Alt-dragging a layer moves a duplicate of it rather than the original.

**Options bar**

| Control                    | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | In this app                                            |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Tool Preset Picker         | The tool icon at the far left of the options bar with a flyout arrow. Clicking it lists that tool’s saved presets; Control-clicking it (Command-clicking on macOS) opens a two-item menu — Reset Tool, which returns the current tool’s options to their defaults, and Reset All Tools, which does the same for every tool. It is the escape hatch for the fact that a tool’s options are the ones you last used, not the ones it shipped with.                                                                                                                                                                | `missing`                                              |
| Auto-Select                | Checkbox that, when on, resolves the target by hit test: the tool selects the topmost layer that actually has pixels under the cursor, rather than moving whichever layer happens to be active.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | `partial` — `src/components/Main/MoveToolArea.tsx:178` |
| Auto-Select: Group / Layer | Menu beside the Auto-Select checkbox choosing what the hit test resolves to. Layer takes the individual layer under the pointer; Group takes the whole layer group that layer belongs to, so a click anywhere on a grouped child moves the group.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | `missing`                                              |
| Show Transform Controls    | Checkbox that puts the transform bounding box and its handles on the currently selected layer without putting the tool into transform mode — the handles simply appear, and they surround every selected object when several are selected. Dragging one of them is what starts the transform, and it is the same handle-driven state Cmd+T opens; the bar swaps to the numeric transform fields while a handle is held.                                                                                                                                                                                        | `partial` — `src/components/Main/MoveToolArea.tsx:123` |
| Align                      | Six buttons, enabled once two or more layers or groups are selected: Top Edges, Vertical Centers, Bottom Edges, Left Edges, Horizontal Centers and Right Edges. Each moves the selected layers so the named edge or center coincides with the extreme of the selection, or with the selection border. Adobe also states the target as two menu commands — Layer > Align against the selected layers, Layer > Align Layers To Selection against the selection border — and the bar control reaches the same two targets through the `Align to` row below.                                                       | `missing`                                              |
| Distribute                 | The distribute row, enabled only at three or more selected layers: the same six edge and center commands to space the layers evenly between the outermost two, plus the Horizontally and Vertically spacing buttons. The two outermost layers are treated as fixed and only the ones between them move.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | `missing`                                              |
| Align to                   | The control that chooses what the align and distribute commands align to: Selection, the default, against the border of the current selection, or Canvas, the whole document. It sits at the right of the alignment group, reached through the three-dot More control, and it changes what the same six buttons do rather than adding a command. Adobe's own account of it is the Canvas route — "To align layers based on the canvas, click the More icon (the three dots) to choose Canvas" — and the Selection default is the state users report as "the alignment is set to 'Selection' and not 'Canvas'". | `missing`                                              |
| Width                      | Numeric text box, in percent, for the layer width. It replaces the Auto-Select controls while a transform is active, and carries a Link icon that is on by default since Photoshop 21.0.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | `missing`                                              |
| Height                     | Numeric text box, in percent, for the layer height, paired with Width through the Link icon so a corner drag scales proportionally.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | `missing`                                              |

**Modifiers**

- **Alt** — Drag a duplicate of the layer or selection instead of the original, leaving the source layer where it was. Printed by Adobe as Alt on Windows and Option on macOS.
- **Shift** — Constrain the drag to a single axis, so a sloppy diagonal snaps to purely horizontal or purely vertical movement.
- **Shift** — Click a layer in the canvas or the Layers panel to add it to the current selection rather than replacing it. Adjacent layers need only Shift-click; noncontiguous layers need Ctrl-click (Command-click on macOS).
- **Arrow keys** — Nudge the active layer by one pixel when nothing is selected on it, or the selection itself by one pixel when there is.
- **Shift+Arrow keys** — Nudge by ten pixels instead of one.

**Shortcuts**

- `V` — Select the Move tool. Tapping the key selects it; holding it springs the Move tool onto the currently active tool for as long as the key is down, and releasing returns to the tool you were on. Spring-loaded switching is a preference (Preferences > Tools > Spring-loaded Tool Shortcuts) and is on by default.

**In this app:** `partial` — The app's Move tool moves and resizes, and the whole gesture is one committed history entry, but almost nothing of Photoshop's bar survives, and what does survive is not merely narrower than Photoshop's: the one canvas overlay the app draws is a resize rectangle where Photoshop draws a transform box, and two of Photoshop's controls are behaviours this app has with nothing on screen to turn them off. That overlay is a divergence rather than a gap, and it is why the verdict is `partial` and not `implemented`. The two rows whose behaviour is welded on are `partial` on exactly that basis, and their `appRef`s point at the behaviour the app performs rather than at a control, because there is no control in the bar to point at. Neither the Auto-Select checkbox nor the Group/Layer menu beside it is rendered, and a search of `src/` and `e2e/` finds no control for either: the tool always resolves the layer under the pointer by hit test and always makes it active, which is Auto-Select: Layer with that state permanently on and the group mode removed — so a grouped child cannot be dragged out of its group, and a click that lands on a transparent part of a layer finds whatever is underneath instead of nothing. There is no Show Transform Controls checkbox either, and the difference is more than cosmetic, because the overlay that does render is a plain resize rectangle drawn by the shared useRect hook — four painted corner handles sitting on eight draggable edges, no rotation zone at all outside the box, no numeric W/H, no reference point — so the geometric half of the tool, which is where Free Transform normally lives, is absent from the Move tool entirely. The align, distribute and align-target rows, the Alt-drag duplicate, the Shift axis constraint, the Shift-click-to-extend and the arrow-key nudge are all missing, which together mean the app can place one layer but cannot line several up. A third divergence is the refusal, which is not a missing feature. The app refuses a press on a bedrock layer, and it separately refuses to move or resize a layer whose own PSD protection flag is set, which is Photoshop's own constraint rather than a divergence: `locked` is written back out as composite and position protection, and the guard sits above every commit kind, so a protected layer cannot be dragged. What the app cannot do is the half that makes the guard reachable — no panel renders a lock control, so the flag only ever arrives on a layer imported from a PSD, and the refusal is silent where Photoshop names the lock. The keyboard is a divergence too, and it is a strange one because the badge looks right. The Move tile declares V in the toolbar mapping, and the app does bind V — but the badge is not what binds it, and the letter-key layer is a separate hand-written table rather than anything derived from the toolbar. Spring-loaded switching does not exist here at all: the handler switches the tool on keydown and nothing listens for the keyup, so holding V cannot borrow the Move tool for one gesture and hand it back. Auto-Align is a different matter, because it is not this tool's control to lose: in Photoshop it is the Edit > Auto-Align Layers command, a dialog with a Projection choice, and the app has no equivalent of it at all. The panel the app does render is its own: the active layer's name, a Merge all button and a hint, none of which Photoshop's Move bar has.
