### Free Transform — the Edit > Free Transform command, not a Tools panel Tool

`transform`

Photoshop's Free Transform (Cmd+T) scales, rotates, skews, distorts, adds perspective or warps a layer in one continuous operation.

Free Transform puts a bounding box around the active layer and lets one continuous operation change its size, angle and shape together, which is the point: rotating and rescaling an image in two steps resamples it twice. Every mode is a drag on that box, and the mode is chosen by right-click menu, by an options-bar button, or by holding a modifier so the box changes behavior mid-gesture. Nothing is written to the document until you commit, so a transform can be abandoned and undone as a unit.

**Options bar**

| Control                                      | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | In this app                                                            |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Width                                        | Numeric text box, in percent, for the layer width. The paired Link icon is on by default since Photoshop 21.0, so a corner handle scales proportionally.                                                                                                                                                                                                         | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Transform/Transform.tsx:254` |
| Height                                       | Numeric text box, in percent, for the layer height, linked to Width by the Link icon.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Transform/Transform.tsx:269` |
| Maintain Aspect Ratio (Link)                 | Toggle between proportional and non-proportional scaling, on by default since Photoshop 21.0. Shift is bound to the same state and inverts it while held.                                                                                                                                                                                                        | `missing`                                                              |
| Reference point location                     | A 3-by-3 grid of squares choosing the pivot, draggable in the document to move the transform origin. The reference point is hidden by default and must be shown from this control; transforms start from the object center until it is moved.                                                                                                                    | `missing`                                                              |
| Rotation                                     | Numeric text box, in degrees, for the rotation angle. The same angle is produced by dragging outside the bounding box, where Shift snaps to 15-degree increments.                                                                                                                                                                                                | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Transform/Transform.tsx:183` |
| H                                            | Numeric text box, in degrees, for horizontal skew. Adobe names the field H: "To skew numerically, enter degrees in the H (horizontal skew) and V (vertical skew) text boxes in the options bar." The pair is absent from the bar when a Smart Object is the thing being transformed.                                                                             | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Transform/Transform.tsx:203` |
| V                                            | Numeric text box, in degrees, for vertical skew — Adobe's V, the other half of the H/V pair above.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Transform/Transform.tsx:218` |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — With a rotation drag outside the bounding box, constrain the angle to 15-degree increments. With a handle drag, toggle proportional scaling off and on, which is what Shift means since Photoshop 21.0.
- **Alt** — Distort relative to the center point of the bounding box, so the opposite handle moves at the same time in the opposite direction. Printed by Adobe as Alt on Windows and Option on macOS.
- **Cmd** — Distort freely by dragging a handle, in any direction, with no constraint. Printed by Adobe as Command on macOS and Control on Windows.
- **Cmd+Shift** — Skew: drag a side handle to slant that side while the opposite side stays parallel.
- **Cmd+Alt+Shift** — Perspective: drag a corner handle so the layer recedes toward one edge, the two sides no longer meeting at a right angle.

**Shortcuts**

- `Cmd+T` — Free Transform. Choosing the Move tool and checking Show Transform Controls enters the same state, which is how a pixel layer gets its box.
- `Cmd+Option+T` — Duplicate the layer or selection and enter Free Transform on the duplicate, leaving the original untouched.
- `Enter` — Commit the transform. Selecting another tool or another layer commits it too.

**In this app:** `partial` — Free Transform is a command, not a tool. The primary evidence is a negative one and it is a good one: a complete, version-stamped inventory of the Photoshop 2026 Tools panel lists every entry in the bar — Move, the marquees, the crop, the pen family, the type tools, the shape tools, Hand, Zoom — and has no Transform entry in it, while Photoshop reaches the operation through Edit > Free Transform or Cmd+T. Adobe's own routing agrees, sending a pixel layer to the Move tool with Show Transform Controls rather than to any transform tool. Note the shape of the menu, because it is two items and not one: Edit > Free Transform is a top-level Edit item, and Edit > Transform is a separate submenu carrying the six single modes — Scale, Rotate, Skew, Distort, Perspective and Warp. One counter-sentence exists on Adobe's marketing copy — "Select the Transform tool by pressing Ctrl + T (Cmd + T for Mac)" — but the very next clause of the same page is "You can also go to Edit > Free Transform": the page names the menu route itself, and uses "tool" for the interactive state rather than for a Tools-panel entry. The app reaches the same command from Edit > Free Transform and from Cmd+T, so both of the routes Adobe documents exist here, and the route matches while the panel does not: it makes the panel in the options bar a different thing from Free Transform's bar, and the two should not be described as the same control set. Colors and Levels went the other way, out of the toolbar and into Image > Adjustments, because they are commands too; `extraTools` in toolbar-mapping.ts is the list of registered tool ids that deliberately carry no rail entry. What the app builds is a fixed-parameter panel for the Image > Transform operations — rotate 90 degrees left, 180 and 90 degrees right, a continuous rotation slider clamped to plus or minus 90, skew X and skew Y in plus or minus 45 degrees, scale X and Y in 10 to 300 percent, and horizontal and vertical flip — plus one projective operation the app calls Trapezoid, a percentage taper that narrows the top or the bottom of the layer about its horizontal centerline. Photoshop's nearest counterpart for that taper is the Perspective mode of Free Transform, reached by Cmd+Option+Shift-drag rather than by a slider, and it is mutually exclusive with every other parameter here: setting Trapezoid resets rotation, both skews and both scales to their defaults, and the processor refuses a trapezoid combined with any retained affine transform rather than composing them. The panel is not a live transform either. There is no bounding box, no handles, no reference point and no commit-on-click-outside; the sliders write a preview through the transient update path and commit when the gesture ends. A drag PREVIEWS while the pointer is down and lands as exactly one history entry when the pointer is released, which is the browser's own native `change` event on a range input and not React's `onChange`, which is the `input` event and fires on every frame of the drag (`src/components/ToolbarsRight/Transform/Transform.tsx:54-69`). The five discrete controls commit in the same place, because a rotate button and a mirror toggle are finished gestures too. A release that moved nothing writes nothing, so a click that lands where it started costs no history entry. The commit is also still reachable by leaving the tool or exporting, and Escape is the only way back: it calls the cancel handler, which deletes the pending preview, resets the panel to its defaults and dispatches nothing, so what remains is the last committed state. The bar itself carries no commit control, no discard control and no Reset control — the whole right-hand column is the two mirror toggles, centered in the slack the three removed text links left behind. Those removals were a HEIGHT fix, not a width one, and the measurement is worth keeping because the reason reads backwards without it: the column is a `flex flex-col` under the mirror toggles, so those controls were stacked rather than laid out across. With all four children it measured 85px inside the strip's fixed `h-[50px]` (`src/components/ToolbarHorizontal/ToolbarHorizontal.tsx:5`) and spilled 35px above and below it. The bar's own width did not change by a pixel across that work — 548px before and after — and a horizontal overflow was never the defect; if it ever becomes one the levers are `w-24`, `w-10` and `gap-4`. Of Free Transform's own bindings, Cmd+T and Escape are wired and Enter does not commit because there is no commit key to bind; the step back Adobe documents for a live transform is absent: "To undo the last handle adjustment, choose Edit > Undo." Warp, Distort and Perspective-as-a-drag have no implementation at all, and the composite order the app declares — scale, then rotation, then skew, all about the untransformed layer center — is fixed, where Photoshop composes handle drags in the order they happen.

### Levels — the Image > Adjustments command, not a Tools panel Tool

`levels`

Photoshop's Levels remaps an image's tonal range through a histogram, a gamma pivot and per-channel black, white and output points.

Levels is the tonal correction tool: it stretches or compresses where the image's darkest and lightest pixels land, and bends the midtones independently of the ends, which is what separates it from a brightness or contrast slider. The histogram above the controls is the working surface — you read where the data actually sits, then move the three input sliders until the blacks reach the black point, the whites the white point, and the middle slider makes the gamma adjustment that sets overall midtone brightness without crushing either end. Every move can be scoped to one color channel, which is how a cast gets removed rather than merely desaturated. The two routes are not equivalent, and Adobe says so: choosing Image > Adjustments > Levels "makes direct adjustments to the image layer and discards image information", while an adjustment layer stays editable.

**Shortcuts**

- `Cmd+L` — Apply the Levels command. Cmd+Option+L re-applies it with the last settings used. Cmd+Shift+L is not a second Levels binding — it is Auto Tone.

**In this app:** `partial` — Levels is an Image > Adjustments command, or an adjustment layer — not a toolbar tool — so it has no rail entry at all: the app reaches it from Image > Adjustments > Brightness/Contrast, named for what it computes, and carries Photoshop's own Levels item in the same submenu as a disabled command this app cannot do. No control of Photoshop's Levels panel is reproduced, and the two sliders that are rendered are not Levels controls at all: Photoshop's Levels has no Brightness and no Contrast slider. The one control whose name the app does borrow is the Reset button, and it does not behave as Photoshop's does. What the app renders is CSS brightness() and contrast() over the encoded pixel values, driven PROPORTIONATELY — one constant factor step per slider step, the response Adobe's own words name for this adjustment in its default mode: 'In normal mode, Brightness/Contrast applies proportionate (nonlinear) adjustments to the image layer, as with Levels and Curves adjustments' — so it is a flat linear multiply and a pivot at mid-gray in encoded space where Photoshop's curve is nonlinear and, for Levels itself, piecewise-linear through three control points with its middle slider moving the midtone at level 128. The two sliders carry Adobe's own travels for that adjustment: Brightness -150 to +150 and Contrast -50 to +100. The Brightness slider is labelled and centred on a neutral of 0, and the proportionality makes that literal rather than approximate: 0 emits exactly brightness(100%), so the panel at its defaults applies nothing at all, and it is the slider's minimum of -150 that emits brightness(0%) and multiplies the whole layer to black — a range-wide multiply, where Photoshop's black point is a threshold that only remaps the pixels below it. The negative half of BOTH sliders is exactly non-clipping, which is the property the removed exponential curve broke by reaching a factor of 0 on Contrast and flattening the whole image to one mid-grey. The positive half is the boundary this engine cannot cross: Adobe's normal mode does not clip in either direction and its response is nonlinear, while CSS brightness() is a clamped pure multiply that cannot create a white that was not already white and contrast() clips every input past 0.5 + 0.5/f. Closing that needs a per-channel lookup table applied per pixel, the same absent mechanism the rest of this entry depends on. There is no black point, no white point, no gamma midtone, no output pair, no histogram, no channel selector, no Auto, no Auto Options and no eyedroppers. Levels works on the document's encoded values rather than a linear-light space — Adobe draws exactly this contrast with Exposure, which does calculate in linear color space — and the app's filter is likewise in whatever space the canvas composite happens to be. A committed adjustment is retained rather than destroyed, and that is the half of the split the app gets right. A committed Levels adjustment is a layer operation, not a rewrite of pixels: the layer's own bitmap is never touched, the commit appends an operation to the layer's operations array and records one history entry, the renderer re-derives the filter from that array on every frame, and undo and redo replay the operation rather than a stored raster. What the app does not have is the other half of the split: the adjustment is not re-editable, so a committed one can only be taken back with undo, which is why the Reset button is gated on an uncommitted preview and restores the panel's own defaults rather than re-opening the adjustment. The engine for all of that is a CSS filter string assigned to ctx.filter on an ordinary HTMLCanvasElement 2D context — the canvas the user is actually looking at, which the renderer builds with document.createElement and draws the layer stack into. The OffscreenCanvas processors in src/tools/levels.ts are not on that path at all: levels and color are registered as commit: 'layer-operation', and the preview and commit paths append the operation and return before any pixel is produced, so those processors are never reached while editing, previewing or committing. The one surface that still applies the string to an OffscreenCanvas 2D context is the durable materializer, which prefers new OffscreenCanvas wherever one exists; no module outside src/contexts/**tests** imports it today, and the OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D.filter support Safari has never shipped is a property of that surface rather than of the canvas this tool edits on. The string is built in one place, so the renderer and that materializer cannot drift, and the test harness exposes filter as a real writable property, so the emitted string is assertable — though the jsdom mock still cannot rasterize it, so no assertion here proves what the filter looks like.

### Black & White — the Image > Adjustments command, not a Tools panel Tool

`color`

Photoshop's Black & White converts a color image to monochrome with six hue-sextant sliders, optionally tinted with a tone color.

Black & White is not a desaturation — it is a weighted mix, and the six sliders are the weights. Each of the six sextants of the color wheel, Reds, Yellows, Greens, Cyans, Blues and Magentas, gets its own control over how bright that family of hues becomes in the result, so a landscape can have a dark sky and a bright sky in the same conversion, and skin can be lifted without touching the greens. Every slider starts at a value that reproduces a conventional conversion — Photoshop opens the adjustment having already applied "a default grayscale conversion to your image" — and dragging one away from that value is the whole technique. Ticking Tint lays a uniform tone color over the monochrome so it reads as toned rather than neutral, which is how a sepia or a split-tone is made from a color original without going back to it.

| On-image adjustment icon | The Targeted Adjustment tool, sitting directly under the Preset option at the top of the panel. Adobe states the gesture as a drag of the icon itself: "Select and drag On-image adjustment icon onto the image to adjust tones." It moves the sextant slider for whichever family of hues dominates the pixels under the cursor, and that one slider moves every area containing those hues rather than a mark you place.                                                                                                                                                      | `missing`                                                       |
| Auto                     | Sets a grayscale mix based on the values in the image itself — Adobe's own words are "Set a grayscale mix based on your image's color values" — so it reads the layer rather than asking you to weight six families by hand.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | `missing`                                                       |
| Tint                     | Checkbox that lays a uniform tone color over the monochrome result, which is what turns a neutral conversion into a toned or sepia one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | `missing`                                                       |
| Tint Color               | The color swatch beside the Tint checkbox. Choosing it opens the Color Picker, and the tone applied is called Tint Color.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | `missing`                                                       |
| Color sliders            | Six sliders, one per sextant of the color wheel, in the order Reds, Yellows, Greens, Cyans, Blues, Magentas. Each sets how bright that family of hues renders in the monochrome. Adobe's own page names the block and nothing inside it — "Color sliders: Drag sliders to adjust gray tones for specific colors" — so both the six family names and their order are third-party, as are their resting values: the default of 40, 60, 40, 60, 20 and 80 is documented, but the pages that print it print only the first three, "Reds set to 40%, Yellows set to 60%, and so on". | `missing`                                                       |
| Reset                    | The reset icon that returns the sliders to their default values, and more generally the panel control that returns the adjustment to its original settings.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Colors/Color.tsx:185` |

**Shortcuts**

- `Shift+Cmd+Opt+B` — Open the Black & White command. Printed by Adobe's shipped shortcut sheet as "Black & White... Opt+Shift+Cmd+B" on macOS, and Ctrl+Alt+Shift+B on Windows; the app binds no shortcut for it.

**In this app:** `partial` — Black & White is an Image > Adjustments command, or an adjustment layer — not a toolbar tool — so it has no rail entry, and the app reaches the same three CSS filters from Image > Adjustments > Desaturate, which is the Adobe command the bar's grayscale slider actually computes. That name is a bounded divergence rather than a match: sepia and saturation are controls Desaturate does not have. Adobe's Photo Filter is a separate command in the same submenu and it is a disabled item, because it is a lens filter with a Density slider and a Preserve Luminosity option and this bar reproduces none of those. No control of Photoshop's seven is reproduced, and the three sliders that are rendered are not Black & White controls: there is no sextant weighting anywhere in the app, so no per-hue decision can be made and the conversion is a flat luminance desaturation rather than a mix. The one control whose name the app shares is Reset, and it does not behave as Photoshop's does: it is disabled unless an uncommitted preview is live, and it restores that panel's own defaults rather than the sextant defaults, so a committed conversion can only be undone. The grayscale slider is the nearest thing to the whole panel and it is the one control that cannot stand in for it, because a hue-weighted mix and a luminance average differ the moment any of the six families is pushed. Sepia is not the Tint checkbox either: Tint lays a uniform tone color over a conversion whose mix you still control, and applying sepia is a second filter stage that tints the whole image rather than replacing its channel weights, so the two can be combined and the result is not the same look. Saturation belongs to no part of Black & White; it is a Hue/Saturation control, and the fact that this app has one is a leftover from the identity question this tool's shape was chosen to answer. Presets, Auto, Tint, Tint Color, the on-image adjustment icon and the six sliders are all absent. As with Levels, the engine is a CSS filter string, and the surface it is assigned to is the visible canvas: the renderer builds an ordinary HTMLCanvasElement, sets ctx.filter from the layer's operations array and draws the layer stack into it. The OffscreenCanvas processors in src/tools/colors.ts are not on the editing, preview or commit path — color is registered as commit: 'layer-operation', so those paths append the operation and return before a pixel is produced — and the committed conversion is retained on the same terms as Levels, with the layer's own bitmap untouched and undo replaying the operation rather than a raster. The string is built once, so the renderer and the durable materializer cannot drift, and the test harness exposes filter as a writable property, so the emitted string is assertable; the jsdom mock still cannot rasterize it, so no test here shows what the filter looks like.

## Eyedropper and draw

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/eyedropper-draw.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/eyedropper-draw.notes.md).

### Eyedropper Tool

`eyedropper` · **I**

Samples a color from anywhere in the image and makes it the foreground color, previewing as you drag and confirming on release.

The Eyedropper reads pixels and hands the result to the color controls, so a color that is already in the image can be matched exactly instead of guessed. A plain click sets the foreground color; Alt-click (Windows) or Option-click (macOS) sets the background color, and the sampled color is also added to the Swatches panel. Sample Size sets the footprint: Point Sample reads the precise value of the one pixel clicked, and the average settings read the mean of a square of pixels around it. A click is not the whole gesture: you can drag the Eyedropper along an area of the image and release once you get the desired color, and the foreground or background color box changes dynamically as you drag along. Separately, and not as part of that gesture shape, holding Alt or Option from any painting tool reaches the Eyedropper temporarily and samples the foreground color at the Eyedropper’s current Sample Size.

**Options bar**

| Control     | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | In this app                                                             |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Sample Size | Sets the sampling footprint, and Adobe enumerates the whole menu: Point Sample "Reads the exact value of the clicked pixel", and 3 by 3 / 5 by 5 / 11 by 11 / 31 by 31 / 51 by 51 / 101 by 101 Average "Reads the average color value within the selected pixel area". There are no Median entries in it. Adobe lists the menu without saying which entry ships selected, and states no default for it; the app seeds Point Sample. | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Eyedropper/Eyedropper.tsx:22` |
| Sample      | Chooses which layers a sample is read from: All Layers, Current Layer, Current & Below, and the No Adjustments variants. Adobe enumerates that menu and states no default for it. Earlier versions expressed this as a `Sample All Layers` checkbox. The app renders no control for it at all, and its `sampleAllLayers` field persists in settings and is refused loudly on click.                                                 | `inert` — `src/tools/settings.ts:226`                                   |

**Modifiers**

- **Alt** — Sets the sampled color as the background color instead of the foreground color — "Select a new background color by holding Alt (Windows) or Option (macOS) and clicking the desired area in the image." The drag form works the same way: held through a drag, the background color box changes dynamically as you drag along and the sample is confirmed on release.

**Shortcuts**

- `I` — Selects the Eyedropper, or temporarily switches to it while held.
- `Shift+I` — Cycles the tools that share the letter: Eyedropper, Color Sampler, Ruler, Note and Count. The app cycles the two of the five it has, the Eyedropper and the Ruler.

**In this app:** `partial` — The app implements the tool without a processor: it is the sole member of the pixel-free set, so it rasterizes nothing, has no `commit` kind, and its `toolsMap` entry carries only an icon and an options bar. A click dispatches a color change and nothing else, so the app records no history entry for a sample and a sample is not undoable — the same class as a zoom, a panel move or a tool switch. `Sample Size` is the one control this bar matches rather than diverges on: all seven of Adobe’s entries are rendered with Adobe’s own labels in Adobe’s order, and the sample itself is Photoshop’s behaviour — an odd-sided square centred on the click, clipped at the canvas edge rather than shifted inward, reduced by an arithmetic mean. Three behaviors diverge. The drag is the first of them: the app’s only handler is `handlePointerDown` (`src/components/Main/EyedropperToolArea.tsx:59`), wired only to `onPointerDown` (`:137`) with no move or up handler anywhere in the file, so the sample is taken at the pointer-down position alone, no color box previews as the pointer travels, and a drag samples its first pixel rather than the one under the pointer at release. `Sample All Layers` is the second: nothing is rendered for it at all. The permanently unchecked, permanently disabled checkbox this bar used to carry is gone — a box that reads as a switch and cannot be used is worse than an absent one — and `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Eyedropper/__tests__/Eyedropper.test.tsx:77` pins that no such control exists. The field itself survives, seeded `false` at `src/tools/settings.ts:226`, and no control anywhere in the app writes it — the only `patchToolArgs` call in this bar writes `sampleSize` (`Eyedropper.tsx:15`) — so the settings state persists and drives nothing, and a click that found it set refuses loudly with a named reason rather than silently sampling the composited canvas and presenting it as the whole document’s (`EyedropperToolArea.tsx:65`). The composited read is the third: the sample always comes from the composited workspace canvas, and no setting narrows it to one layer, because that needs a composite that excludes adjustment-layer corrections. **The Alt modifier is not among the divergences** — it is implemented, and as Adobe states it: `EyedropperToolArea.tsx:133` dispatches `SET_BACKGROUND_COLOR` when `event.altKey` is held and `SET_COLOR` otherwise, so the sampled colour reaches the background swatch on Alt (Windows) or Option (macOS) exactly as in Photoshop, with no platform branch because the modifier is `altKey` on both. The app omits one of Photoshop’s `I` behaviors. There is no spring-loaded switch: `I` selects the tool outright and the keyboard hook has no key-up listener at all, so there is no temporary mode and no return on release. `Shift+I` now cycles the tile, which is the last of the divergences this record used to carry and the only one that was ever about the app rather than about Photoshop: `measurementGroup` in `AppKeyboardShortcuts.tsx` holds the two tools this app has in Adobe’s `I` family, with a `shift: true` twin beside the plain registration, and it replaced a pair of identical `i` registrations of which the second had been dead code on `useKeyboardEvents`’ last-registered-wins. Three of the five tools Photoshop cycles to are still absent — Color Sampler, Note and Count — and they are absent from the cycle rather than listed in it, because a name the app cannot select would make `Shift+I` land on the inert surface. The sampling-ring toggle is deliberately absent from the census above rather than overlooked. Adobe’s two current pages that describe this bar, the tool page and the set-colors page, name only `Sample Size` and `Sample`, so the ring is not a proven gap and is not filed as `missing`; the name is unconfirmed in 27.x, with third-party sources calling it `Show Sampling Ring` and Adobe’s own CS5 help mentioning only "a color sampler ring for the Eyedropper tool" without naming a control. The app has no ring either way, since the ring is a cursor and this repo has no cursor registry at all.

### Ruler Tool

`ruler`

Measures a distance on the canvas: drag a nonprinting line and the options bar reports X, Y, W, H, the angle and the length, with Shift snapping to 45 degrees.

The Ruler answers a question about the image that no other tool answers: how far apart two things are. You drag a line from one point to another and the measurement appears in the options bar and the Info panel — the starting location, the horizontal and vertical distances traveled, the angle relative to the axis, and the total length traveled. The line is a nonprinting overlay: it measures the document and is never part of it, so it creates no history state, cannot be undone, and disappears when you drag it out of the image or clear it. A line already on the canvas is edited in place rather than replaced: drag it by its body to move it, drag either end to resize it, and a press that never moves is a click, which changes nothing. Holding Shift constrains the line to 45-degree increments, which is how a straight edge or a repeated offset is laid out rather than eyeballed. Alt-drag (Windows) or Option-drag (Mac OS) from one end of an existing line pulls a second leg out of it, turning the measurement into a protractor: the bar then also reports the second leg as D2 and re-reads the angle as the angle between the two legs. It shares the I key with the Eyedropper, the Color Sampler, the Note tool and the Count tool, and Shift+I cycles between them.

**Options bar**

| Control               | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | In this app                                                    |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| X, Y                  | The starting location of the measurement, which is where the drag began rather than either end of it. The app reads the pointer-down point directly, so a drag that ends up and to the left of where it started reports the start it was given.                                                                                                                                                            | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Ruler/Ruler.tsx:84`  |
| W, H                  | The horizontal and vertical distances traveled from the x and y axes. Both are magnitudes in the app, so a drag up and to the left reports the same W and H as the drag down and to the right; Adobe prints them as unsigned distances too.                                                                                                                                                                | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Ruler/Ruler.tsx:86`  |
| A                     | The angle measured relative to the axis, in degrees. It is the one readout Adobe exempts from the document unit: "All measurements except the angle are calculated in the unit of measure currently set in the Units & Rulers preference dialog box." With a protractor present the bar re-reads it as the angle between the two legs, which is Adobe's own reuse of the same letter.                      | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Ruler/Ruler.tsx:88`  |
| D1                    | The total length traveled. The app reports it in document pixels, which is the unit available while the app has no Units & Rulers preference; a measurement scale would rescale this number and not the geometry.                                                                                                                                                                                          | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Ruler/Ruler.tsx:89`  |
| D2                    | The second leg of a protractor, and the only readout that appears and disappears with a gesture: it is present once an Alt/Option-drag has pulled a leg out of an existing line and absent before that, rather than reported as zero.                                                                                                                                                                      | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Ruler/Ruler.tsx:93`  |
| Clear                 | Removes the measuring line, which Adobe describes as one of two ways to remove it: "To remove the line, drag it outside the image area or press the Clear button". The app implements both, and the button is greyed while there is no line because there is nothing for it to remove.                                                                                                                     | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Ruler/Ruler.tsx:112` |
| Use Measurement Scale | A checkbox Adobe's Ruler page does not document and this app does not render. The measurement scale itself is an Image > Analysis menu command — "Select Image > Analysis > Set Measurement Scale > Custom", where the Pixel Length and Logical Length are typed — and the app has no Analysis submenu, so the scale does not exist to be switched on. Recorded rather than omitted so the gap is visible. | `missing`                                                      |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the measuring line to 45-degree increments — "Hold down the Shift key to constrain the tool to 45° increments" — which rotates the drag onto the nearest multiple while keeping its length and its direction of travel.
- **Alt** — Pulls a second leg out of an existing measuring line and turns the measurement into a protractor: "To create a protractor from an existing measuring line, Alt-drag (Windows) or Option-drag (Mac OS) at an angle from one end of the measuring line". The drag has to start within eight pixels of one end of the line, which is the app's tolerance and not Adobe's: Adobe states the gesture and not the radius, and without one every Alt-drag anywhere on the canvas would be a protractor. Either end may be the vertex, and which one it was does not move the origin — X and Y keep reporting the point the line was drawn from, because the alternative — swapping the two endpoints to make `end` the vertex — re-reads two of the seven numbers the moment the protractor is pulled from the near end.

**Shortcuts**

- `I` — Selects the Ruler, or the Eyedropper when that is already the selected tool of this tile.
- `Shift+I` — Cycles the tools that share the letter: Eyedropper, Color Sampler, Ruler, Note and Count. The app cycles the two it has and leaves the other three out of the cycle rather than landing on tools that do not exist.

**In this app:** `partial` — The tool is implemented as a pixel-free tool, and that classification is the reason its history behaviour is not a bug. Adobe calls the measuring line a nonprinting line and gives its removals as dragging it out of the image and pressing Clear, neither of which is an undo, so there is no history state to record and no durable operation to replay: the tool has no entry in `toolProcessors.ts` at all and is declared in `PIXEL_FREE_TOOLS` beside the Eyedropper, whose pixel-free status is established rather than assumed. Adobe never states the history rule outright for this tool, so the app-side answer is `HANDOFF.md` §74 naming the Ruler one of the measurement-band tools that commit no pixels and need no durable operation. Four behaviors diverge. The protractor has one gesture of Adobe's two: the Alt/Option-drag is implemented and the double-click half — "or double-click the line and drag" — is not, because Adobe does not say which end of the line the double-clicked leg pivots on and a second gesture that guessed would be worse than the first alone. The measurement scale is missing, as its own control above records, and it is missing with its `Image > Analysis` menu rather than as a checkbox without one. There is no Info panel, so the options bar is the only place the readouts exist; Adobe names both. And the endpoint tolerance for the protractor is eight document pixels, an app decision stated in `src/tools/ruler.ts` rather than presented as Adobe's, because a gesture with no radius at all would make every Alt-drag a protractor and leave no way to start a new measurement; the same radius bounds the drag that MOVES a line by its body, so the two gestures are one contiguous target and the nearer endpoint wins where they meet. What is implemented is all four of Adobe's own gestures — measure, resize, move and protractor — both modifiers, both removals, and all seven readouts. The press that starts a gesture is refused outside the document frame, because the tool area is the whole workspace and a line begun on the pasteboard would report a negative X or Y for a point the user cannot see; a press INSIDE the frame that never moves is a click and changes nothing, so a click neither destroys a line nor leaves a zero-length one that would capture the next drag. The line survives a tool switch, which is Adobe's own sentence rather than an app convenience — "If your document has an existing measuring line, selecting the Ruler tool causes it to be displayed" — so it lives in a module store rather than in the tool area, and it is dropped when the DOCUMENT changes or when the frame does — its size and its origin, because the two fail differently: size alone could not tell two documents apart and the app's own Blank seed is a fixed size, so a line measured on one image would otherwise survive being replaced by another of the same size and be reported over it, while a size alone cannot see the same-size crop that moves the frame's origin, and a measurement is in frame coordinates, so every pixel it names would then be reporting against coordinates the crop had removed. The angle convention is the screen one: 0 degrees along positive x and increasing clockwise, because y grows downward on the overlay and that is how a protractor on the screen reads.

### Draw Tool

`draw`

Photoshop's name for it is **No Photoshop tool — this app’s own tool (nearest Photoshop: Brush tool)**.

This app’s own freehand stroke tool, not a Photoshop tool: a drag becomes a new layer of ink, drawn with a pen, a dashed pen or a spray.

There is no Photoshop tool called Draw, in this app or in Adobe’s Tools panel, so there is no Adobe behavior to describe and none is invented here. What the tool does is this app’s own: a drag pushes one raw pointer coordinate per move onto the stroke, the stroke is drawn as a bezier curve through those coordinates in the foreground color, and the finished stroke is committed as a new layer, so every mark is a separate object that is separately undone and separately deleted. A Pen Type dropdown picks one of three renderers — a solid round-capped stroke, a dashed stroke, and a spray of soft radial gradients — and Size, Opacity and, for the dashed pen only, Dash and Gap shape it. A live preview at the end of the bar draws the current settings, so a stroke can be judged before it is committed. A user coming from Photoshop should reach for the Brush tool for the solid stroke, and should know that this app renders no airbrush control on any tool, so the Spray pen is the nearest thing here to the Brush’s airbrush; there is no Photoshop equivalent to a dashed freehand ink stroke.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | In this app                                                  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Brush Preset picker | Opens the brush tip chooser, and lets the current preset’s Size and Hardness be changed without reopening the Brush panel. The app has no brush tips, so there is no picker and no hardness.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | `missing`                                                    |
| Size                | The diameter of the brush tip, in pixels. Photoshop’s Size runs from 1 to 5000 px; the app’s slider runs from 0.5 to 500 in steps of 0.5.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Draw/Draw.tsx:149` |
| Mode                | The blend mode the stroke’s paint composites with. Default: Normal.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | `inert` — `src/tools/draw.ts:43`                             |
| Opacity             | The transparency of the color applied. As a stroke passes over an area the color does not exceed this level until the button is released; a further stroke adds more. Adobe’s own words are "Opacity of 100 percent is opaque", which is a value rather than a default, and Adobe states no default for the control. The app seeds a lower default per pen — 90% for the solid and dashed pens, 50% for the spray.                                                        | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Draw/Draw.tsx:211` |
| Flow                | The rate at which color is laid down as the pointer moves, so together with Opacity it sets how fast paint builds up under a held button. Adobe states no default for it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | `missing`                                                    |
| Airbrush            | A toggle that keeps the brush laying down color while the pointer is held still, so a stationary stroke builds up to Opacity instead of stopping at one pass. This app renders no airbrush control at any point in the Draw bar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | `missing`                                                    |
| Smoothing           | How much intelligent smoothing is applied to the stroke, 0 to 100: "Set a value between 0 and 100 to control how much smoothing is applied. Lower values apply minimal correction. Higher values result in stronger smoothing but may slightly delay the stroke preview." Adobe names the Brush, Pencil, Mixer Brush and Eraser as the tools it applies to. The app declares the field on the draw args and no Draw-bar control writes it, so the value is always absent. | `inert` — `src/tools/draw.ts:38`                             |

**Shortcuts**

- `[` — Decreases brush Size.
- `]` — Increases brush Size.

**In this app:** `implemented` — No Photoshop provenance is claimed and none is invented: the Tools panel has no freehand-annotation or pen-stroke tool, and this app’s Draw tile sits in the tonal group where Photoshop has no tool at all. The nearest Photoshop tools are the Pen tool family, for path work, and the Brush, for freehand paint. The `shortcut` field on a toolbar entry is display-only and binds nothing: its only consumers are the tile tooltip and the <kbd> in the flyout, and the key bindings live in a separate hand-written table. This tool declares no shortcut. Adobe’s published default-keyboard-shortcut reference gives no letter for a Draw tool, so there is no Adobe binding this app is surrendering; the letters are occupied by this app’s own keymap instead — `W` and `Shift+W` both select the Object Selection tool, and `B` and `Shift+B` both select the Brush — so there is no free key to declare for this tool. It was previously badged `B`, which was wrong twice over — `B` belongs to the Brush in Photoshop, and in this app `B` is bound to the brush group (brush, pencil, color replacement, eraser) with `Shift+B` cycling it, so pressing `B` selected the Brush and could never select this tool. The badge is gone rather than reassigned because a declared shortcut the app does not implement is a falsehood the rail prints, and reassigning it is a product decision about which tool wins the chord. So this tool is reachable by pointer only. Photoshop’s spring-loaded switch is also absent: no key in the table selects this tool, so holding a letter cannot reach it either. The two fields the Photoshop paint bar exposes as Mode and Smoothing are declared on the draw args but unreachable from this bar — no draw control writes either, the default args set neither, and a draw stroke’s layer is forced to Normal by the blend-mode gate that admits only the paint tools. Two app-only controls, Dash and Gap, have no Photoshop counterpart in the paint bar. Three of the Brush bar’s controls diverge rather than go missing. Size is `partial` on its range alone: the slider starts at 0.5 px where Photoshop starts at 1 and stops at 500 px where Photoshop reaches 5000. Opacity is `partial` for the same kind of reason, and the build-up rule is the part that diverges: the value is measured and applied correctly, but a draw stroke is one `beginPath`/`stroke()` over the whole path at the tool’s alpha, so where a stroke crosses itself the color does not compound within that stroke, and Adobe’s rule is that the color does not exceed the set level however many times the pointer crosses the same pixels until the button is released. And the airbrush toggle is `missing` rather than approximate: the Draw bar renders Pen Type, Size, Dash, Gap, Opacity and a preview, and nothing that builds color up under a held button. The Spray pen type is the nearest thing and it diverges twice over — it is reached from the Pen Type dropdown rather than a toggle, and it stamps one soft gradient per sampled point along the drag, so it builds while the pointer is moving and a press that is then held still adds nothing after the single dot it already laid down. The bracket keys Photoshop binds to resize the tip reach no tool here, because this tool is the one the binding could serve and is not in its table: `[` and `]` are registered, but only for the tools `tipSizeField` names — brush, pencil, color replacement, eraser, smudge, dodge, burn and clone stamp — and this tool’s Size writes the same `lineWidth` field the brush uses while being absent from that list, so the two keys are inert for it rather than unbound. And Photoshop’s Shift-constrains-a-freehand-stroke-to-a-straight-line has no implementation here either — the draw area reads no modifier at all, so a Shift-held drag produces the identical freehand path.
